paragraphs: ANCIENT INDIAN HISTORY
Palaeolithic Age
The Palaeolithic culture of India developed in the Pleistocene period or the Ice Age.
Homo sapiens first appeared towards the end of this phase.
Palaeolithic men were hunters and food gatherers.
They had no knowledge of agriculture or pottery.
They used unpolished, rough stones and lived in cave and rock shelters.
Their tools were mostly made of quartzite.
Thus they are also called as Quartzite men.
The age is divided into three phases according to the nature of the stone tools used by the people and change in climate.
Early or Lower Palaeolithic- hand axes, cleavers and choppers.
Humidity decreased. Locations are Soan Valley (Punjab), Belan 	Valley (Uttar Pradesh).
Middle Palaeolithic – flakes- blades, pointers, borers and scrapers. Further decrease in humidity. Locations are Valleys of Soan, Narmada and Tungabhadra rivers.
Upper Palaeolithic – scrapers, burins and bone tools. Warm Climate. Caves and rock shelters of the age have been discovered at Bhimbetka near Bhopal.
Mesolithic Age
Transitional phase between Palaeolithic Age and Neolithic Age.
Climate became warm and dry- this brought changes in flora and fauna.
The Mesolithic people lived on hunting, fishing and food gathering.
At a later stage, they also domesticated animals.
The characteristic tools of the Mesolithic Age are Microliths.
Microliths were small tools made of stone.
Pointed cresconic blades, scrapers etc made up of stones were other important tools.
Adamgarh in Madhya Pradesh and Bagor in Rajasthan provide the earliest evidence for the domestication of animals.
The people of Palaeolithic and Mesolithic ages practiced painting.
Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh is a striking site of Pre-Historic painting of Mesolithic Age.
Neolithic Age
Use of polished stone tools, they particularly used stone axes.
Important sites in India include Burzahom, Mehrgarh, Brahmagiri, Nagarjunakonda etc.
Burzahom dogs were buried with their masters in their graves.
The Neolithic settlers were the earliest farming communities.
They domesticated cattle, sheeps and goats.
Hand made pottery and use of potters wheel first appeared during the Neolithic Age.
Koldihwa in UP is a three fold cultural sequence of Neolithic, Chalcolithic and Iron Age.
Mehargarh in Baluchistan is the oldest Neolithic site in India (7000 BC)
Chalcolithic Culture
The end of Neolithic period saw the use of metals.
Copper was the first metal to be used.
Chalcolithic culture refers to the stone-copper phase.
People also used hand-axes and other objects made up of copper ware.
Primarily rural communities, domesticated animals and practiced agriculture.
They worshipped mother goddess and the bull.
Chalcolithic people were the first to use painted pottery.
Black and red pottery painted with white line design was most popular. Prevalent from 2000 B.C. onwards.
The Malwa ware is considered the richest among the Chalcolithic wares.
Important sites in India are Eran, Malwa, Daimabad, Rangpur, Jorwe (modern Maharashtra), Navdatoli etc.
Wheat and rice produced, also bajra, pulses, cotton.
INDUS VALLEY CIVILIZATION/HARAPPAN CIVILIZATION (2600 BC-1500 BC)
The civilization-part of Proto- history of India and belongs to Bronze Age.
1826 – Charles Masson
Alexander Cunningham-Five decades later, collected seals.
1924 - John Marshall named it Indus Valley Civilization.
By Historians, Harappan Civilization
Contemporaries- Mesopotamia (Tigris and Euphrates, Egypt (Nile) and China (Hwang Ho).
It can be divided into following sub-parts:
Early Phase 3500-2600 BC
Middle (mature) Phase 2600- 1900 BC
Later Phase 1900- 1500 BC
Chalcolithic Period
Harappa- 1921- excavated by Dayaram Sahni - Banks of river Ravi – Sahiwal District of Pakistan.
Mohenjodaro – 1922 – excavated by RD Bannerji – Banks of river Indus – Mound of the dead.
The civilization covered parts of Sind, Baluchistan, Afghanistan, Punjab, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Rajasthan, Jammu and Kashmir and Maharashtra.
Present day- Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Western U.P, Pakistan, some parts of Afghanistan, Sindh, Baluchistan.
SOME IMPORTANT SITES
Manda in Jammu and Kashmir.
Shortugai in Afghanistan.
Harappa In Western Punjab (Pakistan).
Mohenjodaro and Chanhudaro in Sindh.
Kalibangan in Rajasthan.
Lothal and Dholavira in Gujarat.
Banawali and Rakhigarhi in Haryana.
Daimabad in Maharashtra.
Sutkagendor on Makran Coast – Most western site.
Alamgirpur in Western U.P- Most eastern site
Manda in Jammu (river Chenab) – Most northern site.
Daimabad in Maharashtra (river Pravara) – Most southern site.
Capital cities – Harappa, Mohenjodaro.
Port Cities – Lothal, Sutkagendor.
Largest site – Mohenjodaro (Sindh).
Largest Indian site – Rakhigarhi (Haryana)
Main crops – Wheat, barley.
Rice cultivation evidence – Lothal.
Indus- first to produce cotton in the world.
Lion not known to Indus people.
Trade – Mesopotamia, Sumeria, Ur etc.
Iron not known.
Meluha – Name given to Indus.
TOWN PLANNING
Uniform, grid system-rectangular blocks.
Divided into two parts-
Citadel on higher Mound, Western side. Housed public buildings and ruling class.
Settlement on lower eastern side. Inhabited by common people.
Street right angles, criss- cross pattern.
Divided into several residential blocks.
Drainage system well- laid out- made of mortar, lime and gypsum.
Great Bath – Mohenjodaro
Bitumen on the bed.
Drain for outlet of water.
For ritual bathing/ purposes.
Granary- located on West of Great Bath.
For storing grains.
Granary also found at Harappa.
Other crops found – Mustard, peas.
Agriculture
Soil fertile due to inundation in the river Indus and flooding.
They used wooden ploughshare- world’s first ploughed field at Kalibangan and stone sickles for harvesting.
At Lothal and Rangpur, rice husks were found.
Sugarcane was not known to Indus people.
They were the first to produce Cotton in the world, Greek called them Sindon.
Trade
Trade was based on Barter System.
Coins were not evident.
Weights and measures used. Weights made of limestone and steatite etc. generally in cubical shape.
Decimal system was known to them.
Trade flourished with Mesopotamian’s or Sumerian’s (Iraq), Central Asia, Persia, Afghanistan and Bahrain.
Sumerian text refers to trade with Meluha (Indus), Dilmun (Bahrain) and Makan (Makran coast).
Susa and Ur in Mesopotamia, Harappan seals found.
FINDINGS
Bronze image of dancing girl, stone steatite image of bearded man (Mohenjodaro)
Terracotta (fire baked clay) figurines.
Mother goddess – Matridevi or Shakti.
More than 2000 seals.
No representation of  horse on seals.
Most famous seal- Pashupati or Proto – Shiva (Mohenjodaro)
Terracotta cart from Kalibangan.
Hump and humpless bull.
Tools made of stone and bronze. Bronze made by mixing copper and tin.
Copper was mainly from Khetri mines.
Beads and jewellery of gold, silver, precious stone and steatite.
Pottery both plain (red) and painted (red and black).
Seals made of steatite- one horned bull, buffalo, tiger, rhinoceros, goat and elephant are found on most of the seals.
Seals marked ownership of property.
SCRIPT
Not deciphered.
Fish symbol is most represented.
Boustrophedon.
Pro-Dravidian – Oldest script in Indian sub – continent.
Swastika symbol can be traced from Indus civilization.
Oldest deciphered script – Brahmi script.
Brahui dialect- Spoken by Baluchi people in Pakistan today.
Religious Practices
Indus people believed in ghosts and evil forces and used amulets for protection against them.
Fire altars found at Kalibangan (black-bangles) and Lothal (port city).
Lingam and Yoni worship was prevalent.
Snake worship also found.
Trees and other animals were also worshipped.
No temples found but idolatry was practiced.
Chief female deity- Mother goddess (terracotta figure where plant is shown growing out of embryo of woman)
Chief male deity- Pashupati Shiva or Proto Shiva. Sitting in yogic position, having three heads and two horns, surrounded by elephant, tiger, rhino, buffalo and two deers appear at his feet.
Burial
Dead body mostly placed in North-South direction.
Mostly three types of burial-
Complete Burial
Fractional Burial
Cremation
VEDIC AGE (1500 BC – 500 BC)
EARLY VEDIC (RIG VEDIC) PERIOD1500 BC – 1000 BC
They appeared a little earlier then 1500 B.C in India.
Early Vedic people lived in the region of Sapta Sindhu (land of seven rivers).
Late Bronze age to early Iron age.
1500 – 1000 BC : Early Vedic (Rig Vedic)
1000- 500 BC : Later Vedic
Later move into Ganga and Yamuna valley.
They migrated to India in waves and earliest wave represented by Rig Vedic people.
Early Aryans or Vedic people were distinguished by their common language: Indo- European language.
Originally believed to be from the Steppes region of Southern Russia and Central Asia.
We know about them from Rig Veda.
Rig Veda is the earliest text of Indo-European languages and mentions total 40 rivers such as  Yamuna, Vitasta, Asikni, Parushni, Vipasha, Shutudri and Sarasvati etc.
Economy
Early Aryans occupation was mainly pastoralism and agriculture was secondary.
The horse played the most significant role, they possessed chariots driven by horses.
They probably introduced the spoked wheel.
Ploughshare also mentioned in Rig Veda.
Cow was the most important form of wealth and standard unit of exchange.
Most wars were fought for the sake of cows.
The horse was almost as important as cows.
Copper or Bronze age.
The Rig Veda mentions artisans such as carpenter, chariot- maker, weaver, leather worker, potter etc.
Metal working also known.
No clear evidence of trade.
Political Administration
The Tribal Chief was the head of the tribes and was called Rajan.
His post was hereditary but traces of election by the tribal assembly called ‘Samiti’ was found.
Several tribal or clan based assemblies existed such as Sabha, Samiti, Vidatha and Gana.
Even women attended sabha and vidatha.
Samiti was the National Assembly of the people.
Sabha was the council of elders.
Purohita, religious advisor of king, was most important functionary.
Two priests- Vasishtha (conservative) and Vishvamitra (liberal).
Senani, head of the army.
No regular system of taxation, people gave voluntary offerings to the chiefs called- Bali
No regular standing army, only groups of infantry and charioteers.
Vrajapati- the officer who enjoyed authority over a large land or pasture ground.
Gramani- head of the village (later times).
Weapons were mainly made of stone, wood, bone and metal.
Society
Kinship was the basis of societal structure.
Male dominated society-Patriarchal
People gave primary loyalty to the tribe, called Jana or Vis.
Vis divided into grama.
When grama clashed with one another, it is called Samgrama or war.
Kula or griha- term for family.
Monogamy prevalent.
No evidence of child marriage.
Widow re-marriage was practiced.
Varna was the term used for colour of people and four varna’s were present.
Gradually tribal society divided into three groups- warriors, priests and people.
Brahmins- teachers and priests.
Kshatriyas- rulers and administrators.
Vaishyas- peasants, merchants and bankers.
Sudras- artisans and labourers (appeared towards the end of Rig Vedic period)
Rig Vedic gods
They believed in nature worship.
No temples or idol worship.
They performed yajnas in open areas.
Soma was the god of plants and an intoxicating drink is named after him.
Around 33 gods- Indra (war lord/ rain god) called Purandara meaning Breaker of forts.
Important female divinities were Aditi and Usha.
Different gods- Indra (most important god), Agni (fire god), Varuna (water god), Surya, Maruts (storm god) etc.
LATER VEDIC PERIODc.1000 BC – 500 BC
Later Vedic period mainly based on Vedic texts compiled after the age of Rig Veda.
Later Vedic Texts were compiled in the upper Gangetic basin circa 1000-500 B. C.
Iron-around 1000 BC Dharwar district in Karnataka.
Aryans expanded from Punjab to Western UP covered by Ganga- Yamuna Doab.
Bharatas and Purus combined and form the Kurus tribe.
Kurukshetra- Land of the Kurus.
Later Vedas gave three division of India:
Aryavarta- Northern India
Madhyadesa- Central India
Dakshinapatha- Southern India
Gotra – clan appeared in later Vedic period
Dvija – twice born
Vishnu and Rudra became important.
Upanishads became popular.
PGW – Painted Grey ware.
In later Vedic times, people hardly knew the use of burnt bricks.
Polity
Rig Vedic popular assemblies lost importance.
Vidhata totally disappeared.
The term Rashtra indicating territory first appeared.
Formation of large kingdoms and kingship became completely hereditary.
Sabha and samiti continued but character changed and women were no longer permitted to attend sabha.
There were development of judiciary. Chief administered the court.
Sangrihitri- taxes and tributes deposited to him.
War now fought for territory.
Society
The fourfold division of society became more clear.
Initially based on occupation which later became hereditary.
Brahmin- growing ritual added to the power of the priests class.
Rajanyas/Kshatriyas- Warrior class.
Vaishyas- Agriculturists, cattle rearers, traders, artisans and metal workers.
Shudras- Lowest in social hierarchy and born to serve the upper three varna.
Position of women declined.
Polygamy became frequent.
Economy
Agriculture became the chief economic activity but primitive.
Wheat and rice were chief crops, barley also cultivated.
New occupation such as fisherman, washerman, dyer etc emerged.
Copper one of the first metals to be used by Vedic people but also tin, silver, iron now known.
Later Vedic people acquainted with four types of pottery- black and red ware, black slipped ware, painted grey ware and red ware.
Red ware most popular but most distinctive PGW.
Merchants were organized into ganas.
Religion
Indra and Agni lost their former importance.
Rituals became more important for sacrifice.
Yajamana- sacrifice or performer of Yajna.
Prajapati (creator) became the supreme god, Vishnu the protector of people.
Signs of idolatry appear.
Pushan, for well- being of cattle and god of Shudras.
Toward the end of Vedic age, resentment of priestly domination began.
Important rituals by king-
Rajasuya- The king performed this sacrifice which was supposed to confer supreme power on him.
Asvamedha- king performed this which meant unquestioned control over the area, in which the horse ran uninterrupted.
Vajapeya- king performed Vajapeya or chariot race, in which the royal chariot was made to win the race against kinsmen.
Vedic Literature
Veda- root ‘vid’- ‘to know’ or knowledge.
Collection of Vedic hymns or mantras known as Samhitas.
Rig Veda Samhita oldest text – basis for early Vedic Age description.
Samhitas or Vedas
Rig veda
Sama Veda
Yajur Veda
Atharva Veda
Vedatrayi
(Trio of Vedas)
Brahmanas
Aranyakas
Upanishads
Vedic texts are divided between Shruti (hearing) and Smriti (memory)
RIG VEDA
Oldest Veda and oldest text in the world of Indo –European languages.
Collection of prayers/hymns offered to Agni, Indra, Mitra, Varuna and other gods by various sages or poets, composed around 1700 BC.
10,580 (10,462) verses and 1028 hymns.
Consists of 10 mandalas or books ( II to VII are earliest mandalas)
Books I and X seemed to be the latest additions.
Xth Mandala : Purushasukta (defines the four varnas )
Brahmana
Kshatriya
Vaishya
Shudra
SAMA VEDA
From root word ‘Saman’ meaning melodies.
Books of chants or melodies.
Collection of verses
Important for Indian music
1549 verses
Contains Dhrupad Raga
YAJUR VEDA
Book of sacrifices, rituals.
Verse and prose format.
Two texts/recessions : black and white
Krishna Yajur Veda (Black)
Shukla Yajur Veda (White)
ATHARVA VEDA
Book of magic or magical formulae and spells to ward off evil and diseases.
Prose format.
Ritualistic in nature.
II. BRAHMANAS
Composition of a series of texts.
Explanation of mantras and rituals meaning prose commentaries on various vedic hymns.
They explain the meaning behind the social and religious meaning of rituals.
Every veda has several brahmanas attached to it.
III ARANYAKAS
Books of forest
The sages who dwell in the forests explained the Vedic scriptures to their pupils in this form.
Concluding part of Brahmanas.
It provides details of the rishis living in the jungle.
IV. UPANISHADS
Vedanta- end of Veda (800-500 BC)
Mainly appendices to the Brahmanas.
Philosophical discussions and spiritual in nature.
108 Upanishads.
Satyameva Jayate : ‘Truth alone triumphs’ from Mundaka Upanishad.
Oldest Upanishad : Vrihadaranyaka .
LITERATURE (600 BC- 600 AD)
Smriti-Dharma Shastra is the other name, law books written in sloka form. Manusmriti/ Manav Dharma Shastra is the oldest and most famous.
Epics
Ramayana (Valmika)- originally 6000 verses to 12000 and 	then to 24000 verses.
Mahabharata  (Ved Vyasa)-older then Ramayana. 	Originally, 880 verses then to 100,000 verses.
Puranas- means old-18 famous Puranas. Matsya Purana the oldest.
PRE – MAURYAN AGEMAHAJANAPADAS PERIOD
16 Mahajanapadas- Buddhist and Jain literature
Second urbanisation
Punch marked coins – silver and copper.
Two types : Monarchial and Republican (non-monarchical)
Vajji (Vaishali) – most important republican
Lichchhavis (Vaishali) – first republic.
Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti.
Magadha – Rajgir.
Magadha Empire
6th- 4th BC struggle for supremacy among the four Mahajanapadas- Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti.
Magadha emerged the most powerful and prosperous kingdom in North India.
Founder was Brihadratha and Jarasandha but growth started under the Haryanka Dynasty.
Expansion took place under the Shishunagas and Nandas and reached its zenith under the Mauryas.
HARYANKA DYNASTY
Bimbisara (544- 492 BC)
He built the capital city of Rajgir.
Contemporary of Gautama Buddha and Mahavira.
The first king to have standing army for which he was known as Senani.
He strengthened his position by matrimonial alliances.
His three wives were- Mahakosaladevi, Koshala princess, sister of Prasenjit ruler of Kashi; Chellana, sister of Chetaka, princess of Lichchhavi and Khema, princess of Madra clan of Punjab.
He sent his personal physician, Jivaka to his rival Avanti king Mahasena of Ujjain, to cure him of jaundice.
Gandhara ruler of Taxila, Pukku Sati, sent an ambassador to Bimbisara.
Ajatashatru (492-460 BC)
He was son of Chellana and Bimbisara.
He occupied the throne by killing his father.
Adopted aggressive policy of expansion and gained complete control of Kasi.
He destroyed Vaishali- capital of the Lichchhavis- after 16 years of war and sowing discord amongst the people.
He fortified Rajagriha to meet the threat from Avanti.
He built the fort of Rajagriha and Jaladurga (a water fort) at Patali village on the banks of river Ganges.
He patronized the first Buddhist council and Buddha died during his reign.
Udayin (460- 444BC)
He was the son and successor of Ajatashatru.
He built the fort upon the confluence of Ganga and Son rivers at Pataliputra (Patna).
He transferred the capital from Rajgriha to Pataliputra.
He was succeeded by weak rulers such as Anuruddha, Munda and Nag Dasak.
SHISHUNAGA DYNASTY (412-344 BC)
Shishunaga was the minister of Naga Dasak and was elected by the people.
He destroyed the Pradyota dynasty of Avanti-this ended the 100 year old rivalry between the two states.
Avanti became a part of Magadha.
He temporarily shifted the capital to Vaishali.
Kalashoka succeeded Shishunaga.
He transferred capital from Vaishali to Pataliputra.
He convened the second Buddhist Council at Vaishali in 383 BC.
Sabakami was the president of this Council.
NANDA DYNASTY (344- 323 BC)
Considered to be the first non Kshatriya dynasty of Magadha.
Mahapadmananda was the founder of Nanda Dynasty and he was a great conqueror-known as Ekarat or Eka-Chhatra meaning sovereign ruler.
He was also known as Sarvakshatrantaka meaning uprooter of the Kshatriyas by the Puranas.
Ugrasena- owner of huge army by Pali texts.
He is also known as –the first empire builder of Indian History.
He conquered Koshala and Kalinga and from here he brought an image of Jina as victory trophy.
He was succeeded by his eight sons- the last being Dhanananda.
Dhanananda
He was the last Nanda ruler.
Alexander invaded North Western India during his reign in 326 BC but the huge army of Dhanananda prevented Alexander’s army from advancing towards the gangetic valley.
He was referred to as Agrammes or Xandrames in the Greek texts.
Chandragupta Maurya, assisted by Kautilya overthrew Dhanananda to establish the Mauryan dynasty in 321 BC.
POST VEDIC PERIOD (600BC – 400BC)RELIGIONS-BUDDHISM AND JAINISM
BUDDHISM
Founded by Gautama Buddha, Siddharta, Sakyamuni and Tathagata.
Born in 563 BC at Lumbini, Nepal in Shakya Kshatriya clan of Kapilavastu( Piprawah) in Basti district.
Father – Suddhodhana, Mother – Mahamaya (princess from Koshalan dynasty)
He was brought up by his aunt – Mahaprajapati Gautami
Wife – Yashodhara
Son – Rahul
His teachers were Alara Kalama and Udraka Ramputra.
He left home at the age of 29 years after witnessing four things- old man, sick man, dead body and an ascetic.
He attained Nirvana or Enlightenment at 35 years at Bodh Gaya under a Pipal tree on the banks of Phalgu river on the 49th day of meditation.
First sermon(Dharma – chakra – pravatana : turning of the wheel of law) – Sarnath (Near Varanasi) to five of his disciples.
Died – Kushinagar (UP) at the age of 80 years old in 483 BC under a Sal tree.
Buddha’s horse- Kanthaka
Teachings
Buddhism does not recognize the existence of god and soul (atma)
Four noble truths
The world is full of sorrows.
The cause of sorrow is desire.
If desires are conquered all sorrows can be removed (nirvana).
This can be achieved by following the 8-fold path
Ashtangika Marga (Eight fold path)
Right observation
Right speech
Right determination
Right livelihood
Right memory
Right action
Right exercise
Right meditation
Triratnas (three jewels)
Buddha- the enlightened
Dhamma- doctrine
Sangha- order
Code of conduct
Do not covet property of others
Do not commit violence
Do not use intoxicants
Do not speak a lie
Do not indulge in corrupt practices
Belief in Nirvana also known as moksha or salvation.
It refers to the belief in the concept of ultimate bliss, where the person gets freedom from the cycle of birth and death.
Madhyama marga or Madhayama Pratipada (Middle path)- it means that man should avoid the extremes of both life of luxury and life of severe ascetism and should acquire a middle path.
Buddhist councils :-
483 BC – Ajatashatru (Haryanka Dynasty)
383 BC – Kalashoka (Sishunaga Dynasty)
250 BC – Ashoka (Maurya Dynasty)
72 AD – Kanishka (Kushan Dynasty)
Literature :- Mostly written in Pali Language
I. Tripitaka (pitaka- basket)
Sutta Pitaka- Buddha’s sayings
Vinay Pitaka- Monastic Code
Abhidhamma Pitaka- Philosophy of Buddha’s teachings
II. Milindapanho- dialogue between Milinda (Indo- Greek Ruler) and Nagasena( Buddhist Saint)
III. Dipavamsha
IV. Mahavamsha
V. Buddhacharita written in Sanskrit.
Sacred shrines :-
Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Kushinagar, Sravasti, Rajgriha, Vaishali and Sanskya – Ashtathanas.
Architecture :-
Stupa (relics of Buddha), Chaitya (prayer hall) and Vihara (Residence of monks)
Sects
Mahayana (The Greater Vehicle)
Followers believed in heavenliness of Buddha.
Sought salvation with help of Boddhisattvas.
Believed in idol worship and favoured Sanskrit language.
Two sub-sects: Madhyamika (Nagarjuna) and Vijnanavada (Maitreyanath)
Hinayana (The Lesser Vehicle)
It follows original teachings of Buddha.
They sought salvation through self-discipline and meditation.
They did not believe in idol worship.
They used Pali language.
Two sub-sects: Vaibhasika and Sautantrika
Vajrayana
The followers believed that salvation could be attained by acquiring magical powers called Vajra.
Chief divinity- Taras
JAINISM
Founded by Rishabnath
24 Tirthankaras (guru) in Jainism
1st – Rishabdev/Rishabnath
23rd – Parswanath
24th Tirthankara – Vardhama Mahavira or Jina (conqueror)
Father – Siddharta, Mother – Trishala
Wife – Yashoda, Daughter – Priyadarshini
42 years, attained Kaivalya (supreme knowledge)
Kevalin, Jina, Jitendra, Nrigrantha, Arihant, Mahavira
First sermon at Pava
Died – Bihar.
Triratnas/ three ratnas (Way to Nirvana)
Right faith
Right knowledge
Right conduct.
Five vows/ principles :-
Ahimsa – non violence
Satya – non lying
Asteya – non stealing
Apagriha – non possession
Brahmacharya - celibacy
SECTS :-
Svetambara – Sthulabhadra  - white clad
Digambara – Bhadrabahu – naked
Literature :-
Sacred texts were compiled during 6th century, written in Prakrit language. Some are also written in Sanskrit.
12 Angas, 12 Upangas, 10 Parikarnas, 6 Chhedasutras, 4 Mulasutras, 2 Sutragranthas.
FOREIGN INVASIONS
Cyrus of Persia (588-530 BC) was the first foreign conqueror. He enrolled Indian soldiers in Persian army.
516/518 BC – Darius I, grandson of Cyrus invaded north-west India – Achaemenian ruler
Xerxes-successor of Darius-employed Indians in the long war against Greeks.
Indo – Iranian contact boosts trade, cultural exchange.
Kharosthi script
II. Macedonian Invasion
326 BC – Alexander the great destroyed the Iranian empire and marched towards India through Iran.
Ambhi, the ruler of Taxila, readily submitted to Alexander.
He got the strongest resistance from Porus, Alexander defeated Porus in the Battle of Hydaspas on the banks of river Vitasta (Jhelum).
After Battle of Sakala, he proceeded upto Beas to conquer the east but his fatigued army refused to cross.
He placed the North-Western India under the Greek Governor Seleucus Nikator.
Alexander remained in India for 19 months and died in Babylon in 323 BC at the age of 33 years old.
MAURYA PERIOD (322 BC – 185 BC)
The last of the Nanda rulers, Dhanananda was highly unpopular due to his oppressive tax regime.
Also, post-Alexander’s invasion of North-Western India, that region faced a lot of unrest from foreign powers.
Some of these regions came under the rule of the Seleucid Dynasty, founded by Seleucus Nicator I. He was one of the generals of Alexander the Great.
Chandragupta, with the help of an intelligent and politically astute Brahmin, Kautilya usurped the throne by defeating Dhanananda in 321 BC.
Mauryan Empires – Rulers
Chandragupta Maurya
Bindusara
Asoka
CHANDRAGUPTA MAURYA(324/321-297 BC)
He was known as Sandrocottus or Androcottus by Greek scholars.
He dethroned the last Nanda ruler with the help of Kautilya (Chanakya) or Vishnugupta.
He also defeated Seleucus Nikator in 305 BC and Hindukush became the boundary between them and there was matrimonial alliance.
Seleucus sent Greek ambassador Megasthenes to his court, wrote ‘INDICA’.
Chandragupta embraced Jainism and went to Chandragiri Hill at Sravanbelagola with Bhadrabahu, where he died of slow starvation (Salekhana).
He was the first Indian ruler to unite the whole of North India.
BINDUSARA (297-273 BC)
Greeks called him Amitrochates.
He extended the kingdom further to the peninsular region of India as far South as Mysore.
Antiochus I, Seleucid King of Syria sent Deimachuss as ambassador to his court.
Ptolemy Philladelphus of Egypt sent Dionysius as ambassador to the court of Bindusara.
He patronized Ajivika sect.
ASHOKA (273- 232 BC)
He was the greatest Mauryan ruler.
His kingdom extended to the whole sub- continent except the extreme South including Afghanistan, Baluchistan, Kashmir and valleys of Nepal.
261 BC- Kalinga War in the 9th year of rule – Bherigosha (physical conquest) to Dhammagosha (cultural conquest).
He embraced Buddhism under Upagupta.
He sent his son Mahendra and daughter Sanghamitra to Ceylon as Buddhist missionaries with a sapling of Pipal tree.
Ashoka’s Dhamma- was a code of conduct and a set of principles to be adopted and practiced by the people to build up an attitude of social responsibility and preserve the social order.
To pay respect to elders, mercy to slaves and emphasized truth, non-violence and tolerance.
Edict
Ashoka Inscription Details
Major Rock Edict I
Prohibition of animal sacrifice, especially during festive seasons.
Major Rock Edict II
Medical treatment of humans and animals, planting of fruits, medicinal herbs and the digging of wells. Mentions the Pandyas, Satyapuras and Keralaputras of South India.
Major Rock Edict III
Generosity to Brahmins. About Yuktas, Pradeshikas and Rajukas who would go every five years to different parts of his empire to spread Dhamma.
Major Rock Edict IV
Dhammaghosha (sound of Dhamma/righteousness) over Bherighosha (sound of war). The King Ashoka attached greatest value to his duty.
Major Rock Edict V
About Dhammamahamatras. Talks about treating slaves right. A special cadre of officials, Dhamma Gosha were appointed and entrusted with the duty of spreading Dhamma within the kingdom.
Major Rock Edict VI
King’s desire to know about his people’s conditions. About welfare measures.
Major Rock Edict VII
Tolerance towards religions among all sects and welfare measures for the public in his as well as his neighbouring kingdoms.
Major Rock Edict VIII
Ashoka’s first visit to Bodh Gaya and the Bodhi tree (his first Dhamma Yatra). Gave importance to Dhamma tours.
Major Rock Edict IX
Condemns popular ceremonies. Stresses on moral conduct.
Major Rock Edict X
Disapproves of the individual’s desire for fame and glory and stresses on Dhamma.
Major Rock Edict XI
Dhamma is the best policy to follow, which includes respect for elders and concern for slaves and servants.
Major Rock Edict XII
It mentions Mahamattas in charge of women’s welfare, Ithijika Mahamatta and tolerance towards the dhamma of others.
Major Rock Edict XIII

Mentions victory over Kalinga. Mentions Ashoka’s Dhamma victory over Greek Kings Antiochus of Syria (Amtiyoko), Ptolemy of Egypt (Turamaye), Magas of Cyrene (Maka), Antigonus of Macedon (Amtikini), Alexander of Epirus (Alikasudaro). Also mentions Pandyas, Cholas, etc.

The thirteenth rock edict which was issued at the end of the Kalinga war gives a vivid picture of the change of Ashoka from an aggressive and violent warrior to a great lover and preacher of peace. The direct and immediate effect of the Kalinga war was the conversion of Ashoka to Buddhism.
Major Rock Edict XIV
Purpose of rock edicts.

Ashoka Inscription Details
Pillar Edict I
Ashoka’s principle of protecting his people.
Pillar Edict II
Defines Dhamma as minimum of sins, many virtues, compassion, liberty, truthfulness and purity.
Pillar Edict III
Avoiding practices of cruelty, sin, harshness, pride and anger among his subjects.
Pillar Edict IV
Responsibilities of the Rajukas.
Pillar Edict V

List of animals and birds that should not be killed on certain days. Another list mentions animals that should never be killed. Describes release of 25 prisoners. This pillar edict is also known as Delhi-Topra Pillar Edict.
Pillar Edict VI
Dhamma policy of the State (welfare of the people).
Pillar Edict VII
Ashoka’s work for fulfilling Dhamma. Tolerance for all sects. Also, about Dhamma Mahamattas.
NATIVE SUCCESSORS
I. SHUNGA Dynasty (185- 73 B.C)
Pushyamitra Shunga- Commander-in-Chief of last Mauryan ruler- Brihadratha.
He assassinate Brihadratha and founded the Shunga Dynasty.
He ruled from Vidisha(MP) between 185/ 186- 151 BC.
He is considered to be the prosecutor of Buddhism.
But renovated the Barhut Stupa during his reign.
Greek ambassador Heliodorus visited court of fifth Shunga King Bhagabhadra.
The Shungas marked the revival of Hindu tradition and culture, Sanskrit language and Bhagavatism.
Great Sanskrit Grammarian was patronized by them.
Manusmriti compiled during their period.
Last Shunga King was Devabhuti.
II. KANVA DYNASTY (73-28 BC)
It was a minor dynasty founded by Vasudeva Kanva, he killed the last Shunga king Devabhutti.
Capital was at Pataliputra.
All the rulers were Brahmins, last ruler Susarman was assassinated by Andhra King Simuka.
III. SATAVAHANA DYNASTY (60 BC-225 AD)
Considered to be identical to Andhra’s mentioned in the Puranas, founder is Simuka.
They were successors of Maurya’s in Deccan and Central India.
Gautamiputra Satakarni (AD 106-130) was the greatest ruler of the dynasty. He assumed the title Raja raja and Maharaja.
Pulamayi III was the last Satavahana ruler. They were succeeded by Ikshavakus in 3rd century BC.
The Satavahanas were the first to issue land grants to Brahmins. They also promoted Buddhism.
They issued mostly lead coins apart from copper and bronze.
IV. CHEDI/ CHETI DYNASTY
The Hathigumpha Inscription of Kharavela (third ruler of dynasty) gives information about the Cheti’s.
Kharavela was a follower of Jainism.
He recovered Jaina image from Magadha and was famous for constructing residential caves for Jain monks on the Udaigiri Hill near Bhubaneshwar, Orissa.
FOREIGN SUCCESSORS
I. INDO – GREEKS
The first to invade India after the weakening of Maurya Empire.
They ruled in Bactria lying south of Oxus river in area around North Afghanistan so they were also called BACTRIAN GREEKS.
Most famous ruler was Menander aka Milinda (165- 145 BC), capital at Sakala (modern day Sialkot in Punjab).
He was converted to Buddhism by Nagasena, their conversation was recorded in Milindapanho or ‘Questions of Milinda’.
They introduced features of Hellenistic Art – Gandhara School of Art.
They were the first rulers in India to issue coins attributed to kings and the first to issue Gold coins.
Sanskrit term Horshastra is derived from the Greek term horoscope.
II. SHAKAS OR SCYTHIANS (AD 1st- 4th Century)
The Greeks were followed by the Shakas.
They were five branches from Afghanistan, Punjab, Mathura, Ujjain and Deccan.
Most famous ruler in India is Rudradaman (AD 130-150)
He repaired the Sudarshan Lake (constructed by Pushyagupta under Chandragupta Maurya) in semi arid zone of Kathiawar.
He issued the first ever longest inscription in chaste Sanskrit in Junagarh.
III. PARTHIANS (AD 1st – 3rd Century)
Originally from Iran, moved to India and replaced Shakas.
Occupied only a small portion of North- western India.
Most famous king was Gondophernes, during whose reign St. Thomas came to India.
IV. KUSHANAS (AD 1st – 3rd Century)
They were Yuechis or Tocharians nomadic tribe of North Central Asia. They replaced Greeks and Parthians.
Dynasty was founded by Kujala Kadphises.
Second ruler Wima Kadphises issued gold coins.
Kanishka founded the second Kushana Dynasty in India.
Kushanas were the first rulers to issue gold coins on large scale in India.
Kanishka was also known as second Ashoka and was the most famous Kushana ruler.
He had two capitals at Purushpur and Mathura.
He started an era in AD 78 known as Saka Era and is used by government of India.
He patronized the fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir where doctrine of Mahayana form of Buddhism was finalised.
The last Kushana ruler was Vasudeva I.
SANGAM AGE (AD 1st – 3rd Century)
The land south of Krishna river was divided into three kingdoms-
Pandya- Southernmost part of India- Madurai- kingdom famous for pearl and was ruled by a woman(mentioned by Megasthenes).
Famous for trade with Romans and sent embassies to Roman Emperor Augustus and to Trojan.
Cholas- North east of Pandya between Penner and Velar rivers- capital Uraiyur which was famous for cotton trade and Puhar.
Famous for their navy. Trade based on cotton cloth, kingdom destroyed by Pallavas from the north.
Chera- part of Kerala and Tamil Nadu- capital Vanji or Karur- has well- established trade with Romans and built temple of Augustus at Muzris.
SANGAM LITERATURE
Sangam is associated with college or assembly of Tamil scholars and poets which flourished under the royal patronage of Pandyan Kings.
The whole Sangam Age is called Golden Age or Augustan Age.
The father of Tamil literature is Agastya.
Important works:
Tolkappiyam by Tolkappiyar which is a work of Tamil grammar.
Tirukkural or Kural by Tiruvalluvar is sometimes called the Fifth Veda or Bible of Tamil land. It explains the doctrine of Dharma, Artha, Kama and Moksha.
Aggatiyam comprises of grammar of letters and life, in three parts, written by Aggatiyar.
GUPTA PERIOD(319 AD – 540 AD)
After the fall of Kushanas towards middle of 3rd century Gupta arose in Magadha.
Classical Age or Golden Age of ancient India or Hinduism.
They belong to Vaishya caste.
Srigupta founder around 275 AD.
Followed by son Ghatotkacha.
Son of Ghatotkacha, Chandragupta I known as real founder of Gupta empire.
Both assumed title Maharaja.
I. CHANDRAGUPTA  I (AD 319- 335)-  He married Kumaradevi, a Lichchhavi princess and issued Chandragupta I Kumaradevi type gold coins called Dinaras.
He started a new era known as Gupta Era.
He was the first Gupta king to adopt the title Maharajadhiraja.
He issued gold coins.
II. SAMUDRAGUPTA (AD 335-380)
Son and successor of Chandragupta I.
Allahabad Pillar by court poet Harisena enumerated his conquests.
Known as Napoleon of India by VA Smith due to his bravery and generalship.
Samudragupta succeeded by Ramagupta.
III. RAMAGUPTA was a coward who surrendered to Saka invader.
He was the only ruler to issue copper coins.
IV. CHANDRAGUPTA II (AD 380- 415)
The younger brother of Ramagupta who defeated the Saka invader and occupied the throne.
Mehrauli Iron Pillar Inscription(Delhi) records his authority over North- Western India and his conquests.
Virasena’s Udaygiri Cave Inscription refers to his conquests of the whole world.
Ujjain was his second capital.
Fa Hien visited during his time.
He issued silver coins and was the first Gupta ruler to issue silver coins.
He adopted the title Vikramaditya and Sakari in memory of his victory.
His court was adorned by scholars and poets known as Navratna which included Kalidasa, Harisena and Amarsimha.
V. KUMARAGUPTA (AD 415- 455)-He founded the Nalanda University.
During the last year of his reign, Hunas invasion (Turko-Mongol tribe).
He died during the invasion.
VI. SKANDAGUPTA (AD 455- 467)
Last great ruler.
He fought and repulsed the Hunas twice, for which he adopted the title Vikramaditya, mentioned in Bhitari Pillar Inscription.
Sudarshan Lake repaired during his reign and embankments were rebuilt.
Senabhakta-  form of tax (army to be fed by people).
Guptas issued the largest number of gold coins called Dinaras, silver coins Rupayakas.
510 AD- Sati appeared first in Gupta period- Eran Inscription - Bhanugupta
Bhagavad Gita written during this period.
Buddhism no longer received royal patronage during the Gupta period.
Art and architecture flourished-Samudragupta represented on his coins playing Veena.
Images of Vishnu and Shiva and some other Hindu gods seen for the first time.
Beginning of main style of temple architecture namely Nagara style and Dravida(Shikhar style) with Garbagriha.
Idol worship common from Gupta period.
Ajanta and Ellora Caves – Maharashtra; Bagh Caves – MP
Kalidas – Shakuntala, Shakespeare of India.
Manusmriti – Translated into English by William Jones.
HARSHA PERIOD
Pushyabhuti/ Vardhana Dynasty
They were feudatories of Guptas but gained independence after Hunas invasion.
Harsha belonged to Pushyabhuti Dynasty.
Prabhakarvardhana defeated Hunas.
Harshavardhana came to throne in AD 606 and started Harsha Era.
He was also known as Siladitya, Kannauj is his capital.
He was called the last great Hindu emperor of India.
He was defeated by Pulakesin II, Chalukyan king of Vatapi (Deccan) in 618 AD.
Huen – Tsang, Chinese pilgrim visited during his reign.
Banabhatta wrote Harshacharita.
He died in 647 AD.
Vakatakas- Rudrasena II.
Chalukyas- Vatapi, modern Karnataka.
Pulakesin II- Huen Tsang visited during his reign.
Aihole Inscription- Ravikirti (eulogy about his defeat of Harsha)
Chalukyas- Vesara style or Deccan style in Temple Building.
Pallavas- Kanchi.
Mahabalipuram; Dravidian Style.
EARLY MEDIEVAL INDIA
Northern India (Period from c. 750 – 1000 CE)
This period of history was dominated by three political powers:
The Gurjara – Pratihara who ruled western India and the Upper Gangetic plains till the middle of the 10th century.
The Palas who dominated eastern India till the middle of the 9th century.

The Rashtrakutas who ruled the Deccan and also had control over some areas in north and south India. The Rashtrakutas ruled for a comparatively longer time and acted as a bridge between north and south India.

All the above kingdoms were in constant conflict with each other and tried to gain control over the Gangetic region in north India and this struggle between the three kingdoms is referred to as “tripartite struggle”.
The Pratiharas/Gurjara-Pratiharas

The Gurjaras were originally pastoralists and fighters. The epic hero Lakshmana, door-keeper to his brother, was looked upon as their hero. The Pratiharas took on their title which literally means “door keeper”.
The UNESCO World Heritage Site at Khajuraho is famous for the development of the Gurjara-Pratihara style of temple building.
The kingdom was founded by Harichandra (Brahmana) in Jodhpur (southwestern Rajasthan).
The dynasty gained importance in the second quarter of the 8th century, during the rule of Nagabhata Ⅰ.
Nagabhata Ⅰ (c. 730 – 760 CE)
He successfully resisted the invasion of the Arabs and defeated the Arab army during the Caliphate campaigns in India.
Ruled over the areas of Gujarat, Rajputana and Malwa.
Dhruva, the Rashtrakuta king defeated him.
Vatsaraja (c. 780 – 800 CE)
He expanded his rule over a large part of north India.
He made Kannauj (western Uttar Pradesh) his capital.

His expansion policy created enemies for him – Dharmapala (the Pala king of Bengal) and Dhruva (the Rashtrakuta king). With this started the tripartite struggle which continued for about 350 years. However, Pratiharas exercised their control over Kannauj till the last.
Dharmapala (the Pala king) was defeated by Vatsaraja and in turn, he was defeated by Dhruv (the Rashtrakuta king) in the tripartite struggle.
Nagabhata Ⅱ (c. 800 – 833 CE)
Dharmapala (Palas) was again defeated by Pratiharas – Nagabhata Ⅱ, who was later defeated by Govind Ⅲ (the Rashtrakuta king) in the tripartite struggle.
He was succeeded by his son Ramabhadra, who ruled for a short span of time and was succeeded by his son Mihir Bhoja.
Bhoja Ⅰ/Mihir Bhoja (c. 836 – 885 CE)
He is considered to be the popular ruler of the Pratiharas and ruled for over 46 years.
Earlier, he was defeated by the Rashtrakutas, the Palas but later, with the help of his feudatories – he emerged successful and won over the Rashtrakutas and the Palas.
He had his capital at Kannauj, which was also called Mahodaya.
The Barrah Copper Plate inscription mentions a military camp at Mahodaya called Skandhavara.
He was a great follower of Vaishnavism and assumed the title of “Adivaraha”.
As per the Arab travellers, the Pratihara rulers had the best cavalry in India. He was titled “King Baura” by an Arab traveller named Al-Masudi.
Mahendrapala (c. 885 – 910 CE)
He made significant contributions in further extending the Pratihara Empire – reached west to the border of Sindh, north to the Himalayas, east to Bengal and south past the Narmada.
He fought a battle with the king of Kashmir but had to give some of his territories in Punjab which were won by Bhoja.
Adopted the title “Maharajadhiraja of Aryavarta” (Great king of kings of northern India).
An eminent Sanskrit poet, dramatist critic named Rajashekhar adorned his court.
Mahipala Ⅰ (c. 913 – 944 CE)
The downfall of the Pratiharas started during his reign.
The Rashtrakuta king, Indra Ⅲ defeated him and destroyed the city of Kannauj.
The Rashtrakutas took control over Gujarat as is mentioned by Al-Masudi in his accounts – ‘the Pratihara empire had no access to the sea’.
Rajyapala (c. 960 – 1018 CE)
This Pratihara ruler was defeated by the Rashtrakuta king Krishna Ⅲ.
Mahmud Ghazni raided Kannauj and Rajyapala had to flee from the battlefield.
He was killed by Vindhyadhar Chandela.
Yashpala (c. 1024 – 1036 CE)
The last ruler of the Pratihara dynasty.
The subsequent rulers could not revive the dynasty and gradually their feudatories declared independence and the empire was reduced to the area around Kannauj.

In the 11th century CE, the Ghaznavids completely wiped off the Pratiharas from the political map and were succeeded by Chauhans/Chahamanas (Rajputana), the Paramaras/Pawars (Malwa) and the Solankis/Chalukyas (Gujarat).
Palas of Bengal
Around the 8th century CE, Gopala laid the foundation of the Pala dynasty.
Since the names of all the kings ended with Pala, the dynasty came to be known as the Pala dynasty which in Prakrit means “protector”.
The kingdom included Bengal and Bihar.
The important cities of the Pala dynasty included Pataliputra, Monghyr (Munger), Tamralipti etc.

The areas of Bihar and modern east U.P remained a bone of contention between the Palas, the Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas. However, Bihar and Bengal remained mostly under the influence of the Palas.
The Pala kings followed Buddhism essentially, Mahayana and Tantric schools of Buddhism.
Gopala (c. 750 CE)
Founder of the Pala dynasty.
Gopala displaced the later Guptas of Magadha and Khadga dynasty of eastern Bengal.
Follower of Buddhism and built the famous monastery at Odantapuri.
Dharmapala (c. 770 – 810 CE)
During his reign, the Pala dynasty reached great heights.
He conquered large parts of northern India, although he was earlier defeated by the Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas.
His supremacy was accepted by the rulers of both west and south India such as those of Punjab, western hill states, Rajputana, Malwa and Berar.

He was the founder of the Vikramshila monastery near Bhagalpur (Bihar) which had students from all parts of India and also from Tibet. One of the eminent Buddhist scholars Dipankara (also called Atisa) was associated with this university.
He also founded the Somapuri monastery near Paharpur (Bihar).
The renowned Buddhist scholar Santarakshita belongs to his reign.
Devapala (c. 810 – 850 CE)
Devapala extended the Pala empire and included Assam (Kamarupa/Pragyoytishpur), parts of Orissa (Utkala) and modern Nepal.
He claimed to have extracted tribute from the whole of north India – from the Himalayas to the Vindhyas and from the eastern to the western oceans.
His inscriptions claim to have defeated the Hunas, the lord of Gurjaras (probably Mihir Bhoja) and the Dravidas.

Devapala was an ardent follower of Buddhism. According to the Buddhist tradition, the Sailendra dynasty king, Balaputradeva (ruler of Suvarnadvipa which corresponds to the Indonesian), requested Devapala to grant five villages to the monastery at Nalanda.
He accepted the request and appointed Viradeva as the head of the Nalanda monastery.
In the middle of the 9th century, an Arab merchant Sulaiman visited India and called the Pala empire Ruhimi or Ruhima Dharma.
The Pala rule declined in the late 9th century.
The control of Pala rulers over northern India was too short-lived and were defeated in the tripartite struggle. The subordinate rulers of Assam and Orissa declared independence.
Mahapala Ⅰ (c. 977 – 1027 CE)
Dynasty was revived under Mahipala Ⅰ in the late 10th century.
He defended Palas in Bengal and Bihar against Chola invasions but was defeated by Rajendra Chola.
Ramapala (c. 1072 – 1126 CE)
Revived the Pala fortunes in the 11th century and gained control of Kamarup and Kalinga.
The empire became weak by the 11th century.
Vijaysena (Sena dynasty) destroyed the Pala Empire in the 12th century.
The Pala empire is considered to be the last major Buddhist power in the subcontinent.
The Palas built monasteries and great temples in the region.
The Pala period is referred to as one of the golden eras in the history of Bengal.
It brought both stability and prosperity to the region.
The Palas were patrons of Buddhist universities – Nalanda and Vikramashila.
Under the Pala rule, the proto-Bengali language developed which laid the foundation for the Bengali language.
The first literary work of Bengal – the Charyapada which is a collection of mystic Buddhist poems was written in this era.
The Palas had the best elephant cavalry.
The rulers had diplomatic relations with the Srivijaya empire, the Tibetian empire and the Arab Abbasid Caliphate.
The Abbasid coinage has been found at the Pala archaeological sites.
The religion Islam appeared in Bengal during the Pala reign, which was the outcome of the flourishing trade between Bengal and the Middle East.
The Rashtrakutas (c. 753 – 975 CE)
The period between c. 753 – 975 CE witnessed the rise of the Rashtrakutas in the Deccan.
The chief of a Rashtra is the literal meaning of Rashtrakuta.
They were feudatories of the Chalukyas and had their capital at Manyakheta or Malkhed near Sholapur.
In the tripartite struggle, they defeated the Palas and the Pratiharas.
Rashtrakuta Rulers Dantidurga (c. 733 – 756 CE)
He was the founder of the Rashtrakuta dynasty.
He annexed the Chalukya kingdom by defeating Kirtivarman Ⅱ.
Thus, the Rashtrakuta became the paramount power in the Deccan.
He defeated the Gurjaras and captured Malwa from them.
Krishna Ⅰ (c. 756 – 774 CE)
Expanded the kingdom and brought major portions of Karnataka and Konkan under his rule.
He built the magnificent rock-cut monolithic Kailasa temple at Ellora.
Dhruva (c. 780 – 793 CE)
He further extended the empire and all the territories between the Kaveri river and central India came under his domain.
He defeated the Palas of Bengal (Dharmapala) and Nagabhata Ⅱ (Pratihara king).
Govind Ⅲ (c. 793 – 814 CE)
In the tripartite struggle, he defeated Dharmapala (the Pala king) and the Pratihara king Nagabhata Ⅱ.
The Rashtrakuta empire extended greatly during his reign.
He was compared with Alexander the Great.
He made expeditions to the south – the Cholas, the Pandyas and the Cheras paid tribute to him.
Amoghavarsha  Ⅰ (c. 815 – 880 CE)
He built the Rashtrakuta capital-the city of Malkhed or Manyakheda.
He patronised art and literature.
He is called ‘Ashoka of the south’ for his peace-loving nature and his immense interest in art and literature.
Indra Ⅲ (c. 914 – 929 CE)
Grandson of Amoghavarsha. He defeated Mahipala Ⅰ (Pratihara king) and sacked Kannauj.
Krishna Ⅲ (c. 914 – 929 CE)
He was famous for his expeditions.
He built several temples in the conquered territories including the Krishneswara temple at Rameswaram.
After his death, the power of Rashtrakutas declined. In 972 CE, the Rashtrakuta capital – Malkhed was attacked and burnt to ashes.
The Rashtrakutas patronised Shaivism and Vaishnavism and were tolerant towards other religious sects like Jainism and Islam.
MUSLIM INVASIONS
Arab Invasion in India
Al Hajjaj, the Governor of Iraq sent Muhammad-bin-Qasim to India.
He Conquered Sindh.
Battle of Rewar was fought between Muhammad-bin-Qasim and Dahir the ruler of Sindh.
Dahir was defeated.
Sindh and Multan were captured.
Muhammad-bin-Qasim called Multan as ‘The City of Gold’
Jizya was imposed on non-Muslims.
End of Muhammad-bin-Qasim
Caliph Walid was succeeded by Caliph Sulaiman.
He was an enemy of Al-Hajjaj, the Governor of Iraq.
Muhammad-bin Qasim was the son-in-law of Al-Hajjaj, so he dismissed him and sent him to Mesopotamia as a prisoner where he was tortured to death.
For more than 150 years, Sindh and Multan continued to remain as the part of the Caliph’s Empire.
Effects of Arab Conquest
The subjugation of Sindh made way for Islam into India.
The art of administration, astronomy, music, painting, medicine and architecture were learnt by Arabs from our land and they spread astronomy, Indian Philosophy, and numerals to Europe.
The Turkish Invasion in India
In the 8th and 9th centuries, the Turks dominated the Caliphs of Baghdad
They extended their dominion beyond Sindh and Multan into India.
Mahmud of Ghazni
In 1001 A.D. Mahmud of Ghazni invaded India
He was the first Turkish to invade India.
He invaded the Somnath Temple in 1025 A.D., located on the coast of Kathiawar.
Mahmud of Ghazni was one of the greatest Muslim rulers of Asia.
Ghazni died in 1030.
Muhammad of Ghori came up.
Muhammad of Ghori (1149 – 1206)
He was the third Muslim ruler who invaded India.
He became the ruler of Ghori.
He first invaded India in 1175 A.D.
First Battle of Tarain (1191 A.D.)-He seized the fortress of Bhatinda in 1189 A.D. and then progressed into the kingdom of Prithviraj Chauhan.
Muhammad of Ghori was defeated by Prithviraj in the First Battle of Tarain in 1191 A.D.
In the second battle of Tarain in 1192 A.D, the joined forces of the Rajput rulers under Prithviraj were defeated by Muhammad of Ghori.
Prithviraj was held as a prisoner and later put to death.
The Turkish rule began for the first time in Indian history with the end of the Second Battle of Tarain.
Qutb-ud-din Aibak was appointed as the commander by Muhammad Ghori.
Rajput Uprisings
There were many Rajput mutinies between 1193 and 1198 A.D.
Qutb-ud-din-Aibak defeated them and brought many regions under his control.
Muhammad Ghori made Delhi as the capital.
Battle of Chandawar (1194 A.D.)
Muhammad of Ghori defeated Jaichandra, one of the greatest Rajput ruler of Kanauj and killed him in the battle.
Conquest of Bengal and Bihar
Muhammad-bin-Baktiyar Khilji, one of the commanders of Muhammad of Ghori destroyed Vikramasila in 1202 and Nalanda Universities in 1203A.D.
He was assassinated on 25th March 1206 A.D. in Central Asia by some Shia rebels and Khokhars.
He is considered to be the real founder of the Turkish Empire in India because of his various invasions and subjugations of the Rajput territories in North India.
INTRODUCTION
The Delhi Sultanate was an Islamic empire based in Delhi that stretched over large parts of the Indian subcontinent for 320 years (1206–1526).
Five dynasties ruled over the Delhi Sultanate sequentially:
The Mamluk dynasty (1206–1290)
The Khalji dynasty (1290–1320)
The Tughlaq dynasty (1320–1414)
The Sayyid dynasty (1414–1451), and
The Lodi dynasty (1451–1526).
It covered large swathes of territory in modern-day India, Pakistan, Bangladesh as well as some parts of southern Nepal.
MAMLUK /SLAVE DYNASTY
The Slave dynasty ruled from c. 1206 – 1290 CE.
It was also named the ‘Mamluk’ dynasty; the word Mamluk is an Arabic word that means “slave/owned”.
Three dynasties were established during this period. They were –
Qutbi dynasty (c. 1206 – 1211 CE) – Its founder was Qutub-ud-din Aibak.
First Ilbari dynasty (c. 1211- 1266 CE) – Its founder was Iltumish.
Second Ilbari dynasty (c. 1266 – 1290 CE) – Its founder was Balban.
Qutub-ud-din Aibak (c. 1206 – 1210 CE)
Qutub-ud-din Aibak founded the Slave dynasty.
He was a Turkish slave of Muhammad Ghori who played an important part in the expansion of the Turkish Sultanate in India after the Battle of Tarrain.
Muhammad Ghori made him the governor of his Indian possessions.
He raised a standing army and established his hold over north India even during the lifetime of Ghori.
After the death of Muhammad Ghori (c. 1206 CE), Tajuddin Yaldauz, the ruler of Ghazni claimed his rule over Delhi and the governor of Multan, Nasiruddin Qabach wanted independence.
He also had to face many revolts from Rajputs and other Indian rulers.
However, Aibak, by displaying his mighty power as well as other conciliatory measures, was able to win over his enemies.
He defeated Yaldauz and severed all connections with Ghazni and thus founded the Slave dynasty as well as the Delhi Sultanate.
Muslim writers called Aibak “Lakh Baksh” or giver of lakhs because he donated liberally.
He was titled “Sultan” and he made Lahore his capital.
He also started the construction of the Qutub Minar (first storey only) after the name of the famous Sufi saint Khwaja Qutubuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki.
It was later completed by Iltutmish.
Aibak died suddenly while playing Chaugan (horse polo) in c. 1210 CE.
Aram Shah (c. 1210 CE)
Qutub-ud-din was succeeded by his son Aram Shah who was incapable as a ruler.
He was opposed by the Turkish armies and his rule lasted for only eight months.
Iltutmish (c. 1210 – 1236 CE)
Iltutmish belonged to the Ilbari tribe and therefore, his dynasty was named the Ilbari dynasty.
His half brothers sold him as a slave to Aibak who made him his son-in-law by giving his daughter to him.
Later Aibak appointed him as Iqtadar of Gwalior.
In c.1211 CE, Iltutmish dethroned Aram Shah and became the Sultan with the name of Shamsuddin.
He is regarded as the real consolidator of Turkish rule in India.
During the first ten years of his reign, he mostly concentrated on securing his throne from his rivals.
The commanders of Muhammad Ghori like Yaldauz, Qabach of Multan and Ali Mardan of Bengal and Bihar rose against him.
Iltutmish defeated Yaldauz in the battle of Tarain (c. 1215 CE) and also drove away Qabach from Punjab.
In c. 1220 CE, the leader of the Mongols, Temujin, popularly known as Chengiz Khan, started his march towards Central Asia.
He defeated Jalal-ud-din Mangabarni, the ruler of Khwarizm.
Mangabarni escaped from the Mongols and sought asylum from Iltutmish.
Iltutmish refused to provide him shelter in order to save his empire from the onslaught of the Mongols.
This diplomatic policy of Iltutmish helped him to save his empire from the wrath of Chengiz Khan.
Iltutmish brought Bengal and Bihar back into the Delhi Sultanate.
He also suppressed the Rajput revolts and recovered Ranthambore.
Iltutmish was a great statesman.
In c. 1229 CE, he received ‘mansur’, the letter of recognition from the Abbasid Caliph by which he became the legal sovereign ruler of India.
He completed the construction of Qutub Minar at Delhi, the tallest stone tower in India.
He also introduced the Arabic coinage in India and the silver tanka which became a standard coin in medieval India.
The silver tanka remained the basis of the modern rupee.
Iltutmish organised Turkan-i-Chahalgani, a new class of the ruling elite of forty powerful military leaders.
He nominated his daughter as his successor.
Ruknuddin Feroz Shah (c. 1236 CE)
He was the eldest son of Iltutmish who ascended the throne with the help of nobles.
When the governor of Multan revolted, Ruknuddin Feroz Shah marched to suppress the revolt.
Using this opportunity, Iltutmish’s daughter Raziya with the help of the Amirs of Delhi seized the throne of the Delhi Sultanate.
Raziya Sultan (c. 1236 – 1239 CE)
Raziya Sultan was the first and only female ruler of medieval India’s Sultanate period.
Raziya appointed an Abyssinian slave, Malik Jamal-ud-din Yaqut as master of the Royal horses (Amir-i-akhur).
The recruitment of a few other non-Turks to important positions aroused resentment among the Turkish nobles.
Raziya Sultan discarded the female apparel and held the court with her face uncovered which further created resentment.
She even went hunting and led the army.
In c. 1240 CE, Altunia, the governor of Bhatinda (Sirhind)  revolted against her.
Raziya alongside Yaqut marched against Altunia, but on the way, Turkish followers of Altunia murdered Yaqut and took Raziya prisoner.
In the meantime, the Turkish nobles put Bahram, another son of Iltutmish on the throne.
However, Raziya won over her captor, Altunia and after marrying him, proceeded to Delhi.
But she was defeated and killed on the way by Bahram Shah.
Bahram Shah (c. 1240 – 1242 CE)
The fall of Raziya Sultan paved the way for the ascendancy of ‘the Forty’.
During the reign of Bahram Shah, there continued the struggle for supremacy between Sultan and the nobles.
The Turkish nobles supported Bahram Shah in the beginning but later became disordered and during this unrest, Bahram Shah was killed by his own army.
Alauddin Masud Shah (c. 1242 – 1246 CE)
He was the son of Ruknuddin Feroz Shah and nephew of Raziya Sultan.
After the death of Bahram Shah, he was chosen as the next ruler.
However, he was incompetent and incapable of handling the affairs in the government and was replaced by Nasiruddin Mahmud.
Nasiruddin Mahmud (c. 1246 – 1265 CE)
He was the grandson of Iltutmish who was young and inexperienced.
He had ascended the throne with the help of Balban/Ulugh Khan, a member of Chahalgani (the Forty) who himself assumed the position of regent.
He married his daughter to Nasiruddin and therefore, the real power lay in the hands of Balban.
Balban was powerful in administration but he had to face the intrigues of his rivals in the royal court.
In c. 1265 CE, Nasirruddin Mahmud died and according to some historians, Balban poisoned him and ascended the throne.
Balban (c. 1266 – 1286 CE)
Balban’s experience as a regent made him understand the problems of the Delhi Sultanate.
He knew that the real threat to the monarchy was from the nobles called “The Forty”.
He, therefore, was sure that by enhancing the power and authority of the monarchy, he could solve the problem.
According to Balban, the Sultan was God’s shadow on earth, Zil-e-Ilahi and the recipient of divine grace, Nibyabat-e- Khudai.
Balban enhanced the power of the monarchy.
He introduced rigorous court discipline and new customs like prostration (sijda) and kissing the Sultan’s feet (paibos) to prove his superiority over the nobles.
He introduced the Persian festival of Nauroz to impress the nobles and people with his wealth and power.
He stood forth as the champion of Turkish nobility.
He excluded non-Turks from administration and Indian Muslims were not given important positions in the government.
To monitor the activities of the nobles he appointed spies and developed an efficient spy system.
Balban was determined to break the power of ‘The Forty’.
He spared only the loyal nobles and eliminated all.
Balban had to deal with internal as well as external problems.
The Mongols were looking for an opportunity to attack the Sultanate, the Indian rulers were ready to revolt at the smallest opportunity.
To handle all these problems, he adopted a stern policy and organised a strong central army to deal with internal issues and also to repel the Mongols.
He established a separate military department, Diwan-e-arz and reorganised the army.
Balban paid more attention to restore law and order instead of expanding his kingdom.
The governor of Bengal revolted against Balban.
He sent his forces to Bengal and Tughril Khan was beheaded.
He appointed his son Bughra Khan as the governor of Bengal.
In the northwest, the Mongols reappeared and Balban sent his son Prince Mahmud against them. But the prince was killed in the battle and it was a moral blow to Balban.
He died in c. 1287 CE. He was one of the main architects of the Delhi Sultanate.
However, he could not fully safeguard India from the Mongol invasion.
Kaiqubad (c. 1287 – 1290 CE)
Kaiqubad was the grandson of Balban and was made the Sultan of Delhi by the nobles. He was soon replaced by his son, Kaimur.
In c. 1290 CE, Feroz, the Ariz-e-Mumalik (the minister of war) murdered Kaimur and captured the throne.
He took the title of Jalal-ud-din Khilji and established the Khilji dynasty.

Jalal-ud-din Khilji (c. 1290 – 1296 CE)
Jalal-ud-din Khalji was the founder of the Khalji dynasty.
He was 70 years old when he assumed power.
The Khilji’s were of mixed Turkish-Afghan descent, they did not exclude the Turks from high offices but the rise of the Khiljis to power ended the Turkish monopoly of high offices.
He tried to mitigate some of the harsh aspects of Balban’s rule.

He was the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate who clearly put forth his view that the state should be based on the willing support of the governed and that since the large majority of the population in India were Hindus, the state in India could not be an Islamic state.
He adopted the policy of tolerance and avoided harsh punishments.

For instance, Malik Chhajju, nephew of Balban was allowed to remain the governor of Kara. When Chhajju revolted, it was suppressed but he was pardoned. When the thugs (robbers) looted the country, they were allowed to go after a severe warning.
In c. 1292 CE, when Malik Chhaju revolted again, he was replaced by his nephew and son-in-law, Alauddin Khilji.
During the reign of Jalal-ud-din Khilji, Alauddin invaded Devagiri and accumulated enormous wealth.
During the reception in c. 1296 CE, he treacherously murdered his father-in-law near Kara and usurped the throne of Delhi.
He made generous gifts to the nobles and soldiers to win over them.
Alauddin Khilji (c. 1296 – 1316 CE)

Alauddin Khilji was the nephew and son-in-law of Jalal-ud-din Khilji. He was appointed as the Amir-i-Tuzuk (Master of ceremonies) and also Arizi-i-Mumalik (minister of war) during the reign of Jalaluddin Khalji.
He followed Balban’s policy of governance that was quite contrary to Jalaluddin’s policy of tolerance.
He was convinced that the general prosperity of the nobles, intermarriage between noble families, inefficient spy system and drinking liquor were the basic reasons for rebellions.
Therefore, he passed four laws:
The public sale of liquor and drugs was totally banned.
The intelligence system was re-organised and all the secret activities of the nobles were immediately reported to the Sultan.
He confiscated the property of the nobles.
Social gatherings and festivities without the permission of the Sultan were not allowed. By such stringent rules, his reign was free from rebellions.
Military Campaigns of Alauddin Khilji
Alauddin maintained a huge permanent standing army. He sent his army six times against the Mongols.
The first two were successful but the third Mongol invader, Khwaja came up to Delhi but was stopped from entering the capital city.
The next three Mongol invasions were also dealt with severely and thousands of Mongols were killed.
The north-western frontier was fortified and Ghazi Malik (Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq) was appointed as the Warden of Marches to protect the frontier.
Conquest of Gujarat – Alauddin Khilji sent an army under two of his generals, Nusrat Khan and Ulugh Khan to capture Gujarat in c. 1299 CE.
The ruler Rai Karan and his daughter escaped while the queen was caught and sent to Delhi.
Malik Kafur, a eunuch was also taken to Delhi and later he was made the military commander.
Conquest of Rajputana
After capturing Gujarat, Alauddin’s attention turned towards Rajputana.
Ranthambore – It was considered to be the strongest fort of Rajasthan.
Initially, the Khalji army suffered losses and Nusrat Khan even lost his life.
In c.1301 CE, the fort fell to Alauddin.
The Rajput women committed Jauhar or self-immolation.
Chittor – Alauddin next turned against Chittor.
It was another powerful state of Rajputana.
In c. 1303 CE, Alauddin stormed the Chittor fort.
According to some scholars, Alauddin attacked Chittor because he coveted Padmini, the beautiful queen of Raja Ratan Singh.
Raja Ratan Singh and his army fought bravely but were defeated.
The Rajput women including Rani Padmini performed Jauhar.
This Padmini episode was graphically mentioned in the book Padmavat written by Jayasi.
Malwa and others – In c. 1305 CE, under the able leadership of Ain-ul-Mulk, the Khalji army captured Malwa.
Ujjain, Mandu, Chanderi and Dhar were also annexed.
After this, Alauddin Khilji sent Malik Kafur to the south and himself attacked Siwana.
Raja Shital Deva, the ruler of Siwana fought valiantly but was defeated.
In c. 1311 CE, Jalore – another Rajput kingdom was annexed.
Thus, by c.1311 CE, Alauddin Khilji became the master of north India and captured large parts of Rajputana.
Conquest of Deccan and the far South – Alauddin’s greatest achievement was the conquest of Deccan and the far south.
This region was ruled by four important dynasties – Yadavas of Devagiri, Kakatiyas of Warangal, Hoysalas of Dwarasamudra and the Pandyas of Madurai.
Alauddin sent Malik Kafur to lead the Khalji dynasty invasions to south India.
In c. 1306 – 1307 CE, Malik Kafur attacked Devagiri.
The ruler of Devagiri, Rai Ramachandra surrendered and was treated honourably.
He was given a district of Gujarat and one of his daughters was married to Alauddin.
In c. 1309 CE, Malik Kafur launched his campaign against Warangal. Its ruler Prataparudra Deva was defeated and an enormous booty was collected from him.
Malik Kafur’s next target was the Hoysala ruler Vira Ballala Ⅲ.
He was defeated and a huge booty was seized and sent to Delhi.
Kafur then marched against the Pandyas.
Kafur seized enormous wealth from the Pandya kingdom.
According to Amir Khusrau, Malik Kafur reached as far as Rameshwaram, built a mosque there and returned to Delhi with huge wealth.
Alauddin honoured Malik Kafur by appointing him Naib Malik of the empire.
Alauddin Khilji died in c. 1316 CE.
Although the Sultan was illiterate, he patronized poets like Amir Hasan and Amir Khusrau.
He built a famous gateway known as Alai Darwaza and constructed a new capital at Siri.
Administration of Alauddin Khalji
Military Reforms – Alauddin Khalji maintained a large permanent standing army and paid them in cash from the royal treasury.
He introduced the system of dagh (branding of horses) and prepared huliya (descriptive list of soldiers).
In order to have maximum efficiency, a strict review of the army from time to time was carried out.
Market Reforms –
Alauddin established four separate markets in Delhi-
One for grain (mandi);
another for cloth, sugar, dried fruits, oil and butter;
third for horses, cattle and slaves, and
the fourth market for miscellaneous commodities.
Each market was under the control of a high officer called Shahna-i-Mandi.
The supply of grain was ensured by holding stocks in government storehouses.
There were regulations in place to fix the price of all commodities.
A separate department called Diwan-i-Riyasat was created under an officer called Naib-i-Riyasat.
Every merchant was registered under the market department.
There were secret agents called munhiyans who sent reports to the Sultan regarding the functioning of these markets.
The Sultan also sent slave boys to buy various commodities to check prices. Any violation of the Sultan’s orders resulted in severe punishment.
No hoarding was permissible and even during famines, the same price was maintained.
Land Revenue Administration – Alauddin took important steps in the land revenue administration.
He was the first sultan of Delhi who ordered measurement of land.
Land revenue was collected in cash which enabled the Sultan to pay the soldiers in cash.
His land revenue reforms provided a basis for the future reforms of Sher Shah and Akbar.
The state officer measured the land and fixed land revenue accordingly.
Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah (c. 1316 – 1320 CE)
After the death of Alauddin Khilji, Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah (one of the sons of Alauddin) ascended the throne.
He abolished all the harsh regulations of his father.
He was not able to run the administration efficiently and was murdered.
Nasiruddin Khusrau Shah (c. 1320 CE)
He killed Mubarak Shah.
His reign did not last long.
The governor of Dipalpur, Ghazi Malik killed Khusrau Shah and ascended the throne of Delhi under the title of Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq in c. 1320 CE.
He was the only Hindu convert to sit on the throne of Delhi.

Tughluq Dynasty (c. 1320 – 1414 CE)
This dynasty is also called Qaraunah Turks, as the father of Ghazi Malik was a Qaraunah Turk in origin.
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq/Ghazi Malik (c. 1320 – 1325 CE)
Founder of the Tughlaq dynasty.
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq laid the foundation for Tughlaqabad (a strong fort) near Delhi.
It is believed that Jauna Khan treacherously killed his father and ascended the throne with the title Muhammad bin Tughlaq in c. 1325 CE.
Muhammad Bin Tughlaq/Jauna Khan (c. 1325 – 1351 CE)
He was a very attractive character in the history of medieval times because of his ambitious schemes and novel experiments.
However, his novel experiments and enterprises failed miserably as they were far ahead of their time.
He introduced many reforms.
Transfer of Capital – Muhammad bin Tughlaq wanted to shift his capital from Delhi to Devagiri so that he might be able to control south India better.
He forcibly moved the entire population to the new capital, Devagiri which was renamed as Daulatabad.
After two years, the Sultan shifted back to Delhi due to the scarcity of water supply in Daulatabad.
The distance between the two places was more than 1500 kilometres and many people died during the rigorous journey in summer.
Token Currency – In c. 1329 CE, Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced a token currency, made of copper to replace gold and silver coins.
It was modelled based on the Chinese example (Kublai Khan issued paper money in China).
Very few people exchanged gold/silver for copper and the tokens were easy to forge which led to heavy losses.
Later on, Muhammad bin Tughlaq repealed his verdict and all coins were redeemed in gold/silver, making the treasury empty.
Taxation in Doab – The failure of the above two experiments resulted in a huge loss of money.
In order to improve the financial condition, Muhammad bin Tughlaq increased the land revenue on the farmers of the doab land between the Ganga and Yamuna rivers.
It was an excessive and arbitrary step on the farmers.
A severe famine struck the region at that time which made the farmers revolt.
However, the harsh steps taken by Muhammad bin Tughlaq crushed the revolt.
Agricultural Reforms – He launched a scheme by which takkavi loans (loans for cultivation) were given to the farmers to buy seeds and to extend cultivation.
He set up a separate department for agriculture, Diwan-i-amir-Kohi.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq was the only Sultan of Delhi who had received a comprehensive literary, religious and philosophical education.
He was very tolerant in religious matters.
He maintained diplomatic relations with far off countries like Iran, Egypt and China.
The famous traveller Ibn Batuta (author of Safarnama Rehla) visited India during this period (c. 1334 CE).
During the latter part of Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s reign, the kingdom witnessed a spate of rebellions by the nobles and provincial governors.
In c. 1336 CE, the Vijaynagara kingdom was founded.
In c. 1347 CE, the Bahmani kingdom was established.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq died in c.1351 CE due to the worsening of his health condition.
According to Barani, Muhammad bin Tughlaq was a mixture of opposites.
His reign marked the beginning of the process of its decline.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq (c. 1351 – 1388 CE)
After the death of Muhammad bin Tughlaq in c.1351 CE, Firoz Shah Tughlaq was chosen as the Sultan by the nobles.
He appointed Khan-i-Jahan Maqbal, a Telugu Brahmin convert as wazir (Prime Minister).
Military Campaigns
After ascending the throne, he focussed on strengthening his position over north India instead of claiming his authority over south India and Deccan.
He led two expeditions to Bengal which were unsuccessful and as a result, Bengal became free from the control of the Delhi Sultanate.
Administrative Reforms
He ran his administration in accordance with the advice of the ulemas.
He pleased the nobles and assured hereditary succession to their properties. Thus, the iqta system was revived and was also made hereditary.
He levied taxes as per the teachings of Islam.
Jiziya was imposed on non-Muslims.
He showed intolerance towards Shia Muslims and Sufis.
He regarded Hindus as second-grade citizens and in this respect, he was the precursor of Sikander Lodi and Aurangzeb.
He was the first sultan to impose an irrigation tax.
But at the same time, he also built a number of irrigation canals and wells.
He developed royal factories called karkhanas in which thousands of slaves were employed.
He also increased the number of slaves by capturing the defeated soldiers and young persons.
There were around one lakh eighty thousand slaves during his reign.
New towns were built during his reign. The famous one being Firozabad near Red Fort (now called Firoz Shah Kotla).
Ashokan pillars from Meerut and Topara were brought to Delhi during his reign.
Diwan-i-Khairat, a new department was established to support orphans and widows.
Free hospitals like Dar-ul-Shifa was also established.
Firoz himself authored the book, Futuhat-e-Firozshahi.
He died in c. 1388 CE and after that, the struggle for power between the Sultan and nobles started again.
His successors (like Muhammad Khan, Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq Shah Ⅱ, Abu Bakr Shah, Nasiruddin Muhammad) had to face the rebellions of the slaves created by Firoz.
In the following years, the Delhi Sultanate disintegrated and many provinces like Gujarat and Malwa declared independence.
The invasion of Timur in c. 1398 CE, further aggravated the situation.
Timur was a Mongol leader of Central Asia, head of Chagatai Turks.
When Timur entered Delhi there was barely any opposition.
He sacked Delhi for three days killing thousands of people and gathering huge wealth.
He withdrew from India in c. 1399 CE and his invasion gave a death blow to the Tughlaq dynasty.

Khizr Khan (c. 1414 – 1421 CE)
Before Timur left India, he appointed Khizr Khan as governor of Multan.
He captured Delhi and founded the Sayyid dynasty in c. 1414 CE.
He did not adopt the title of Sultan and was content with Rayat-i-Ala.
He is considered to be an important ruler of the Sayyid dynasty.
He tried to consolidate the Delhi Sultanate but in vain.
He died in c. 1421 CE.
The Sayyid Dynasty (1414-1451 A.D.)Khizr Khan (1414- 1421 A.D.)
He was the founder of Sayyid Dynasty.
He did not swear any royal title.
He was the Governor of Multan.
He took advantage of the disordered situation in India after Timur’s invasion.
In 1414 A.D. he occupied the throne of Delhi.
In 1421, he died.
Mubarak Shah, Khizr Khan’s son succeeded him.
Mubarak Shah (1421-1434 A.D.)
He is first Sultan ruler to appoint Hindu nobles in the court of Delhi.
He constructed “Mubarakbad” City on the banks of the river Jamuna.
Muhammad Shah Mubarak’s nephew succeeded him.
Muhammad Shah (1434-1445 A.D.)
He defeated the ruler of Malwa with the help of Bahlul Lodi the Governor of Lahore.
He conferred Bahlul Lodi with the title Khan-i-Khanan for help in defeating the ruler of Malwa.
Later Ala-ud-din Shah succeeded him.
Ala-ud-din Shah (1445-1457 A.D.)
He was not a strong ruler.
Ala-ud-din Shah was removed from the throne by Bahlul Lodi in 1457 A.D. who was the Governor of Lahore.
Delhi was captured by him and he was sent to Badaun.
Ala-ud-din Shah died in Badaun in 1478 A.D.

Lodi Dynasty (c. 1451 – 1526 CE)The Lodhis/Lodis were the last ruling dynasty of the Sultanate period and the first to be headed by the Afghans, who ruled over Sirhind when the Sayyids ruled in India.
