YOUNG BENGAL MOVEMENT
Founded by Henry Vivian Derozio, teacher at the Hindu College between 1826 and 1831.
His followers were known as the Derozians and their movement as the ‘Young Bengal Movement’.

The movement attacked old traditions and decadent customs, advocating women’s rights and education and educating the public on the current socio-economic and political questions through press and public associations.
ARYA SAMAJ
It was founded by Swami Dayanand Saraswati & it was a revivalist movement in the late 19th century India (1875).
Dayanand opposed a ritual-ridden Hindu religion and called for basing it on the preaching of the Vedas. Only Vedas, along with their correct analytical tools, were true.
The Arya Samaj as a whole opposed conversion of Hindus to Islam and Christianity and therefore advocated re-conversion of recent converts to Hinduism. This process was called Shuddhi.

It means the re-conversion of those Hindus who had once been willingly or forcibly converted into other religions, but were now willing to come back into the fold of Hinduism, also it prevented further conversion.
RAMAKRISHNAN MISSION
Swami Vivekananda established Ramakrishna Mission in 1897 and set up a Math at Belur, Howrah, West Bengal.
PRARTHANA SAMAJ
Founded in 1867, in Bombay by Dr. Atmaram Pandurang & it was an off-shoot of Brahmo Samaj.
It was a reform movement within Hinduism and Justice M.G. Ranade and R.G. Bhandarkar joined it in 1870 and infused new strength to it.
Mahadev Govind Ranade, also ran the Deccan Education Society.
THEOSOPHICAL SOCIETY
Madam H.P. Blavatsky laid the foundation of the movement in the United States in 1875 and later Colonel M.S. Olcott joined her.
In 1882, they shifted their headquarters to India at Adyar.
After the death of Olcott, Annie Besant was elected as its     President.
She founded the Central Hindu University at Varanasi in 1898, which was later developed into the Benaras Hindu University by Madan Mohan Malaviya.
SATYA SHODAK SAMAJ
It was launched by Jyotiba Phule in Maharashtra in 1873, to save the lower castes from the Brahmins.
He wrote ‘Gulamgiri’ and ‘Sarvajanik Satyadharma Pustak’.
Political Organisations before INC
The Bangabhasha Prakasika Sabha was formed in 1836 by associates of Raja Rammohan Roy.

Zamindari Association/Landholders Society by Dwarkanath Tagore at Calcutta in 1837 to safeguard the interests of the landlords. Although it was limited in its objectives, it marked the beginning of an organized political activity and use of methods of constitutional agitation for the redressal of grievances.
Bengal British India Society founded in 1843- George Thompson, Dwarkanath Tagore and Chandra Mohan Chatterjee.
British Indian Association- both Landholders’ Society and Bengal British India Society merged in 1851, founded by Debendranath Tagore in Calcutta. Radhakanta Deb was first President.
The East India Association by Dadabhai Naoroji in 1866 in London.
The Indian League by Sishir Kumar Ghosh  in 1875 in Calcutta.
The Indian Association of Calcutta by Surendranath Bannerjee and Anand Mohan Bose in 1876 in Calcutta.
Poona Sarvajanik Sabha in Poona in 1870 by MG Ranade, GV Joshi and SH Chiplunkar.
Madras Mahajan Sabha by M. Viraraghavachari, B. Subramaniya Aiyer and P. Ananda Charlu.
Bombay Presidency Association by Badruddin Tyabji, Pherozshah Mehta and KT Telang in 1885.
THE INDIAN NATIONAL MOVEMENTS
THE INDIAN NATIONAL CONGRESS
Indian National Congress formed in 1885 by AO Hume.
INC first meeting GOKULDAS TEJPAL SANSKRIT COLLEGE, 28th Dec’ 1885 in Bombay.
First INC president- Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee
72 delegates attended
First organized Indian National Movement on an all India scale.
Venue Pune but shifted to Bombay due to Cholera outbreak.
1890- Kadambini Ganguly, first woman graduate of Calcutta University to address the Congress Session.
Safety Valve Theory
First President- WC Bonnerjee
First Woman President- Annie Besant(1917)
First Indian Woman President – Sarojini Naidu (1923)
First Muslim President – Badruddin Tayabji (1887)
Gandhi President – Belgaum, 1924
Nehru President – Lahore, 1929
Subhash Chandra Bose – Haripura, 1938; Tripuri 1939
JP Kripalani- during Independence
1885-1905 Moderate Phase
Three P’s- Prayer, Petition, Protest
Development and consolidation of national unity irrespective of race, caste, religion and province.
Passing of Indian Councils Act of 1892- which allowed some members to be indirectly elected by Indians, but keeping the majority intact.
Moderate leaders

DADABHAI NAOROJI, BADRUDDIN TAYABJI, MG RANADE, WC BANNERJEE, SN BANNERJEE, PHEROZESHAH MEHTA, MADAN MOHAN MALVIYA, TEJ BAHADUR SAPRU, GK GOKHALE, ANAND MOHAN BOSE, RASH BEHARI GHOSH, P. ANANDA CHARLU, RC DUTT, S SUBRAMANIYAM AIYER etc.
They worked to create a strong public opinion to arouse consciousness and national spirit.
They persuaded the British Government and British public opinion to introduce reforms in India.
1905-1919 Extremist Phase
Dissatisfaction with the methods and achievements of moderates.
Growing consciousness about the exploitative character of the British rule.
Reactionary policies of Curzon- University Act (1904), Indian Official secrets Act (1904) to restrict freedom of press and partition of Bengal in 1905.
Extremists gave the idea of India’s independence the central place in India’s politics.
Extremists Leaders
LALA LAJPAT RAI, BAL GANGADHAR TILAK, BIPIN CHANDRA PAL-LAL,BAL,PAL;
AUROBINDO GHOSH, CHAKRAVARTI BOSE, CHIDAMBARAM PILLAI, T PRAKASHAM etc.
Promotion of Swadeshi and Boycott of foreign goods.
Non-Cooperation with Britisher’s (Passive Resistance).
Partition of Bengal (1905)
Lord Curzon announced partition of Bengal- creating east Bengal and Assam out of rest of Bengal.
The objective was to set up gulf between Hindus and Muslims.
The partition came into force on 16th Oct’ 1905- Day of National Mourning.
The Indian National Movement entered its second phase after the Partition of Bengal.
British reason-Bengal province was too big to be efficiently administered.
The INC and the nationalists of Bengal firmly opposed the Partition.
Within Bengal, different sections of population- Zamindars, merchants, lawyers, students and even women rose up in spontaneous opposition to the partition of their province.
The nationalists could see that it was a deliberate attempt to divide the Bengal’s territory on religious grounds as for eastern part Muslims will be in Majority and for the Western part, the Hindus.
Rabindranath Tagore composed the National song- Amar Sonar Bangla- adopted as National Anthem by Bangladesh in 1971 after its liberation from Pakistan.
The Anti-Partition Movement
The Anti- Partition movement was initiated on 7th August, 1905.
Massive demonstration against the partition was organized at the Town Hall in Calcutta.
Banaras Session of INC in 1905- GK Gokhale- first call for Swadeshi.
Meeting of INC at Calcutta on 7th August, 1905 - Resolution to boycott of British goods.
The Swadeshi and Boycott (1905-1908)
Originated from Anti-Partition Movement- mass meetings were held all over Bengal, use of Swadeshi or Indian goods and boycott of foreign goods were proclaimed and pledged.
Public burning of foreign cloth were organized and shops selling foreign cloth were picketed.
Emphasis was placed on self-reliance or Atmashakti- this resulted in flourishing of nationalist poetry, journalism, self-reliance and opening of many National Educational Institutions.
Nationalist Educational Institutions were founded in Bengal such as Bengal Technical Institute, Bengal National College.
BC Pal and Chidambaram Pillai led Vande Mataram Movement in Madras.
Lala Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh led the movement in Punjab.
Syed Haider Raza led movement in Delhi.
Dadabhai Naoroji at Calcutta Session of INC in 1906 declared Self-Government or Swaraj as the goal of Indian people.
Muslim League
The Muslim League was set up in 1906 by Aga Khan, Nawab Mohsin Ul Mulk and Nawab Salimullah of Dhaka.
The League supported partition and opposed the Swadeshi Movement, demanded special safeguards for Muslim community and separate electorates for Muslims.
Surat Split (1907)
The INC split into two groups at Surat Session of 1907 presided by Rash Behari Bose.
Extremists were led by Lal, Bal and Pal.
Moderates by GK Gokhale.
The moderates demanded mild constitutional reforms, economic relief, administrative re-organization and protection of civil rights.
The extremists were dissatisfied with the movement of moderates, they realised the true nature of British was exploitative.
Morley-Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act of 1909)
Number of elected members in the imperial and provincial legislative council increased.
Separate electorates introduced for Muslims.
Non-official members to be elected indirectly.
Thus, election introduced for the first time.
Legislatures could pass resolutions, ask questions and supplementaries and vote for separate items on the budget.
One Indian to be appointed in the Viceroy’s Executive Council.
Satyendra Sinha was first Indian member appointed to the executive council.
1911- Annulment of partition and capital shifted from Calcutta to Delhi- Lord Hardinge II tenure.
Ghadar Party
Formed by Lala Hardayal, Taraknath Das and Sohan Singh Bakhna in 1913.
Indian revolutionaries in the US and Canada formed the Ghadar (Rebellion) Party in 1913 aka Pacific Coast Hindustan Association.
Most of the members were Punjabi Sikh peasants and ex-soldiers who migrated.
The party was built around the weekly paper Ghadar.
Headquarter at San Francisco.
The First World war provided the Ghadarites opportunity to free India.
Komagata Maru Incident (1914)
It was a Japanese Steam ship that carried Sikh and Muslim Immigrants from Punjab to Vancouver, Canada.
The ship was forced to return to India by Canadian authorities and docked at Budge Budge, Calcutta.
Police considered them a threat and tried to arrest some leaders and open fired on them.
Some passengers died in the incident.
Home Rule Movement (1916)
The Home Rule League was pioneered on lines of a similar movement in Ireland.
Muslim League supported the movement.
Its objective was to work for social and political reforms.
Tilak’s Home Rule Movement started in April,1916 at Poona, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Central Province and Berar excluding Bombay.
He gave the slogan “Swaraj is my birth right and I shall have it.”
Newspapers- Mahratta (English) and Kesari (Marathi) were organs of Home Rule.
Annie Besant’s Home Rule League started at Adyar in September 1916 with George Arundale as its Secretary.
Newspapers- New India and Commonweal.
The rest of India including Bombay.
She was arrested on June 1917 and released on September 1917.
Lucknow Session (1916)
Lucknow Session of INC was presided by Ambika Charan Majumdar.
Moderates and Extemists were united.
Congress and Muslim League signed a pact known as Lucknow Pact or Congress League Pact.
They put up a common political demand for representative government and dominion status, before the government.
Congress accepted the League’s demand for separate electorates.
AUGUST DECLARATION (1917)
Presented by Montague on August 1917, also known as Montague Declaration.
It proposed the increased participation of Indians in the administration and the development of self-governing institutions in India.
Montague-Chelmsford Reforms (1919)
Also known as Government of India Act, 1919.
Dyarchy introduced.
Provincial subjects divided into Transferred and Reserved subjects.
Rowlatt Act (1919)
In 1919, a Sedition Committee headed by Justice Rowlatt led to the formation of ‘Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act’ (Rowlatt Act).
The Act authorized the government to imprison any person without trial and conviction by the Court of Law for two years.
The law also enabled the government to suspend the right of Habeas Corpus, which had been the foundation of Civil Liberties in Britain.
It led to a country wide agitation and marked the foundation of Non-Cooperation Movement.
Gandhi founded Satyagraha Sabha on Feb and launched the Rowlatt Satyagraha on 6th April, 1919.
During March and April 1919, the country witnessed a remarkable political awakening.
There were hartals, strikes, professions and demonstrations.
Gandhi
Gandhi returned to India in January 1915.
He did not join any political organization and toured the country.
During 1917 and 1918, he was involved in three struggles.
CHAMPARAN SATYAGRAHA (1917)- First Civil Disobedience Movement.
To look into the problems of indigo planters (tinkathia system).
AHMEDABAD MILL STRIKE 1918- FIRST HUNGER STRIKE.
To settle disputes between the mill owners of Ahmedabad and the workers.
KHEDA SATYAGRAHA 1918- First Non- Cooperation Movement. Due to failure of crops, the farmers, with Gandhi, withheld the revenue to get remission based on revenue code.
Jallianwala Bagh
The dissatisfaction against Rowlatt Act led to mass agitations.
A large unarmed crowd had gathered on 13th April, 1919 at Amritsar(Punjab) in the Jallianwala Bagh, to protest against the arrest of their popular leaders Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr. Satyapal.
General Dyer ordered his army to open fire on the people.
Jallianwala Bagh was a large open space garden which was enclosed on three sides and had only one exit.
The troops closed the exit and shoot into the crowd. Large number were killed and wounded.
Rabindranath Tagore returned his knighthood in protest.
Hunter Commission was appointed to inquire into it.
On 13th March,1940- Sardar Udham Singh killed Dyer at Coxton Hall, London.
The Khilafat Movement (1919-1922)
Turkey (Ottoman Empire) allied with Germany and Austria against Britain in First World War.
The Indian Muslim regarded the Sultan of Turkey as their spiritual leader, Khalifa.
After the war, the British removed the Khalifa from power and fragmented Turkey.
Muslim in India started the Khilafat Movement in India, for restoration of Khalifa’s position.
The leaders were Ali brothers, Maulana Azad, Hakim Ajmal Khan and Hasrat Mohani.
All India Khilafat Conference was held at Delhi in Nov 1919.
Gandhi saw this as an opportunity to bring about Hindu-Muslim unity against British, although CR Das opposed it initially.
In June 20, an all-party conference met at Allahabad.
The meeting was attended by number of Congress and Khilafat leaders.
In this meeting, a programme of non-cooperation towards the government was declared.
This included boycott of titles conferred by the govt, boycott of civil services, army and police, i.e., all govt services.
Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-1922)
It was the first mass base political movement under Gandhi.
The decision to not cooperate in the most peaceful manner with the govt. and its laws, was endorsed at the annual session of the Congress held at Nagpur in 1920.
The Nagpur Session also made changes in the constitution of the Congress.
The Tilak Swarajya Fund started financing the Non-Cooperation Movement.
Anti-Rowlatt agitation, Jallianwala Bagh tragedy, Khilafat Movement, general economic distress during and after the war were the reason for Non-Cooperation Movement.
The Movement envisaged boycott of school, colleges, law courts, foreign cloth and advocated the used of Charkha.
Boycott of the visit of Prince of Wales in November 1921.
Popularisation of Charkha and Khadi by Congress volunteers.
The movement demanded Swaraj or self rule and redressal of the Punjab wrongs and Khilafat issue.
Lala Rajpat Rai organized educational boycott in Punjab.
CR Das, Motilal Nehru, Saifuddin Kitchlew, Aruna Asaf Ali etc gave up their legal practice.
The Congress Session at Ahmedabad in December 1921 decided to launch a Civil Disobedience Movement.
But before it could be launched, Chauri Chaura incident took place on February 1922.
The incident compelled Gandhi to withdrew the Non-Cooperation movement.
Swarajists vs No-changers
Major development in Indian politics occurred between 1922-1928.
Differences arose among leaders after the withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation movement.
CR Das and Motilal Nehru advocated for council entry.
They wanted the nationalist should end the boycott of legislative council, enter them, obstruct their working according to official plans.
Exposed  their witnesses, transformed them into arenas of political struggle and thus used them to arouse public enthusiasm.
They were called Pro-changers.
Sardal Vallabhai Patel, Dr. Ansari Babu, Rajendra Prasad and others opposed council entry.
They were known as no-changers.
CR Das and Motilal Nehru formed Congress-Khilafat Swarajya Party in December 1922.
CR Das was the president and Motilal Nehru the Secretary. It worked within the Congress.
In 1923 election, the Swarajist’s won 42 seats out of 101 elected seats in the central legislative assembly.
Simon Commission (1927)
The British Govt. appointed the INDIAN STATUTORY COMMISSION known popularly as Simon Commission in 1927.
Its chairman was Sir John Simon, to go into the question of further constitutional reform.
The committee had to review the working of the Dyarchy system introduced by Montague-Chelmsford Reform of 1919.
It was to report to what extend a representative Govt. can be introduced in India.
All the members were white.
The Indians protested due to the exclusion of Indians and in the fear that the foreigners would discuss and decide upon India’s fitness for self Govt.
The National Congress decided to boycott the commission in its Madras session in 1927, presided by Dr. Ansari.
The Muslim League and Hindu Mahasabha decided to support the Congress.
The Commission’s arrival in India on 3rd February 1928 was met with powerful protest.
The Commission was greeted with hartals and black flag demonstration under the slogan “Simon Go Back”.
The Govt. used brutal suppression and police attacks to break the popular opposition.
Lala Rajpat Rai was severely beaten and injured in a Lathi charge at Lahore.
He succumbed to his injuries on 17th November 1928.
Nehru Report (1928)
Nehru Report was tabled in 1928 by Motilal Nehru.
It was to meet the challenge of the Simon Commission by all important Indian leaders and parties by getting together and trying to evolve an alternate scheme of Constitutional Reforms.
It was the first major Indian effort to draft a constitutional framework for whole of India with lists of Central and provincial subjects and Fundamental Rights.
However, the recommendations was on clear on whether the goal was Dominion Status or Complete Independence.
Members were- Tej Bahadur Sapru, SC Bose etc
Nehru Report demanded responsible Govt both at Centre and in the provinces.
But it advocated dominion status not complete independence.
It demanded Universal suffrage.
It rejected separate electorates.
It proposed Muslim reservation in Centre and Provinces, where they are minority.
It recommended equal rights for women.
Freedom to form union and disassociations of the state from religion in any form.
Demanded reorganization of the North-West provinces on linguistic basis.
Jinnah’s 14 points(9th March,1929)
Jinnah did not accept the Nehru Report and drew up a separate list of fourteen demands known as 14 points of Jinnah.
Lahore Session (1929)
Presided by Jawaharlal Nehru.
The session passed a resolution of Poorna Swaraj (Complete Independence) as it ultimate goal.
On 31st Dec, 1929; the newly adopted Tri-colour flag was hoisted on the banks of river Ravi.
26th Jan, 1930 was fixed as the First Independence Day.
The session also agreed on Civil Disobedience under Gandhi and decided to boycott the First Round Table Conference.
Civil Disobedience Movement (1930)
Gandhi placed an ‘Eleven point ultimatum’ before Irwin for administrative reforms before starting the civil disobedience movement.
He stated that if Lord Irwin accepted them, then there will be no agitation.
The civil disobedience movement started on 12th March 1930 by Gandhi with Dandi March.
78 chosen followers walked with Gandhi from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi, nearly 375 km a village on Gujarat seacoast.
Salt production had geographical limitations.
In other parts of the country, the movement included picketing of liquor shops, defiance of certain laws, refusal of taxes etc.
One notable feature was the wide participation of women.

The movement under the leadership of Khan Abdul Gaffar Khan known as Frontier Gandhi, the Pathans organised the society of Khudai Khidmatgars ( servants of God) known popularly as Red Shirts pledged to non-violence and freedom struggle in Peshawar.
Garhwali soldiers refused to open fire on non-violent mass demonstrations.
In North-east India Manipur took part and in Nagaland ,Rani Gaidilieu, 13 years old responded to the call of Gandhi. She was arrested in 1932 and sentenced to life imprisonment.
She was released only after the independence of India.
Chittagong Armoury raided by Surya Sen in 1930.
A raid on Dharsana Salt Works by Sarojini Naidu, Imam Saheb and Maniklal Gandhi.
Rajagopalachari in Madras led a march from Trichinopoly to Vedaranyam along the Coromandal Coast.
K Kelappan in Kerala march from Calicut to Payannur.
The government adopted ruthless repression, Lathi charges and firing on unarmed crowd of men and women.
Over 90,000 Satyagrahis including Gandhi and other Congress leaders were imprisoned.
Congress was declared illegal.
The British govt. summoned the First Round Table Conference in 1930 in London, to discuss the report of Simon Commission. But Congress boycotted the conference.
First Round Table Conference (1930)
Congress boycotted the conference and its proceedings proved abortive.
Muslim League was represented by Mohammed Ali, Agha Khan, Fazlul Haq, MA Jinnah.
Hindu Mahasabha by Moonje and Jayakar.
Liberals such as Tej Bahadur Sapru, Chintamani and Shrinivas Shrastri appeared.
Princes of Hyderabad and Mysore attended it.
The govt. make attempts to negotiate an agreement with the Congress as no results came out with the Congress boycotting it.
Sapru, Jaykar and Srinivas Shrastri initiated talks between Gandhi and the govt.
The negotiation between Irwin and Gandhi was held on 5th March 1931, which came to be known as Gandhi-Irwin pact or Delhi pact.
Under these pact, the govt. agreed to release all non-violent political prisoners and agreed to the right to make salt for consumption.
The Congress was to suspend Civil Disobedience Movement and take part in Second Round Table Conference.
Karachi Session (1931)
It endorsed the Gandhi-Irwin pact
The session also passed a resolution on Fundamental Right and NEP ( National Economic Programme) with the efforts of Nehru and Bose.
6 days before this session, Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were executed.
Second Round Table Conference (1931)
Gandhi went to England in September 1931 along with Sarojini Naidu, Mahadev Desai, GD Birla and Madan Mohan Malviya to attended the conference.
The British govt. refused to concede the basic nationalist demand for freedom on the basis of the immediate grant of dominion status with complete control over defence, external affairs and finance.
Gandhi resumed the Civil disobedience movement on his return in 1932 and finally withdrew it in 1934.
Poona Pact (COMMUNAL AWARD) 1932
British PM Ramsay McDonald announced the proposal on minority representation known as COMMUNAL AWARD in 1932.
Under this the depressed classes, Muslims, Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo Indians, women and backward classes were to be considered a minority.
They would be entitled to the right of separate electorate.
Gandhi reacted strongly to the proposal as he considered the depressed class as integral part of Hindu society.
He thought there was no need to protect the depressed classes through representation.
The need was to eradicate untouchability.
In protest Gandhi resorted to fast unto death in Yervada Jail (Poona) against the separate electorate.
This resulted in the signing of Poona Pact between Gandhi and Ambedkar on 25th Sept.1932
147 seats were to be allotted to the depressed classes in the provincial legislature as against 71 provided and also for adequate representation of depressed classes in Civil services.
Gandhi coined the word ‘Harijan’ for depressed classes and their upliftment became his prime concern.
All India Anti- Untouchability League was started in Sept.1932.
Gandhi decided to begin a 21 day fast on 8th May 1933 for self purification for the Harijan cause.
Third Round Table Conference 1932
The Congress did not participate.
The discussion led to Govt. of India Act 1935.
Govt. of India Act 1935
The discussions of the Third Round Table Conference and Simon Commission Report led to the passing of the Act.
It provided for the establishment of-All India Federation and  a new system of govt. for the provinces on the basis of provincial autonomy.
It abolished the Council of India, established by the Govt. of India act 1858.
The act provided for a Federal Court and Federal Bank.
The Congress rejected the 1935 Act and demanded convening of constitution elected on the basis of adult franchise to frame a constitution for independent India.
Second World War
Lord Linlithgow declared India to be at war without prior assent of the Central Legislature.
The Congress was angered and resigned in the wake of the war.
Congress agreed to support Britain only in return of independence being granted.
The Viceroy promise only to grant this after the war, the Congress ministries resigned in October to November 1939 in protest.
The Muslim League observed 22nd December 1939 as Deliverance Day.
The Viceroy refused to accept for establishment of responsible govt. at the Centre by the Congress.
But the British govt. was desperate for Indians active cooperation in the war effort.
To secure Indian cooperation, it sent to India in March 1942 a mission headed by Cabinet minister Sir Stafford Cripps and before that the August Offer.
August Offer 1940

Viceroy Linlithgow proposed – Dominion Status in the unspecified future, a post war body to enact constitution, expansion of Governor-General’s council with representation of the minorities, establishment of war advisory council.
Congress rejected the offer as there was no suggestion for a national govt. but the Muslim League accepted it.
Individual Satyagraha (1940)
Congress rejected the August Offer because they were convinced that the British would not modify their policy in India.
Gandhi decided to start the Individual Satyagraha in Sept.1940.
Vinoba Bhave was the first Satyagrahi, followed by Nehru and Brahma Dutt.
Delhi Chalo Movement began.
Cripps Mission (1942)
Cripps Mission reached India in March 1942.
They proposed Dominion Status to be granted after war.
Constitution making body to be elected from provincial assemblies and nominated by the rulers in case of Princely states.
Individual princes could sign separate agreement with the British.
The British however would control the defence for war period.
The British Govt’s refusal to immediately accept the Congress demand of forming national govt. was the cause of failure of the mission.
The British govt. undertook to accept and implement the constitution on two conditions- any provinces unwilling to accept the constitution could form a separate union with separate constitution.
The new constitution making body and the British govt. would negotiate a treaty to sort out matters arising out of transfer of power to Indian hands.
Gandhi termed these proposal as a post-dated cheque in a crashing bank.
Though Cripps proposal failed but it provided legitimacy to the demand for Pakistan by accommodating it in the provision for provincial autonomy.
Quit India Movement 1942
All India Congress Committee at Bombay met on 8th August 1942 and passed the famous Quit India Resolution.
It also proposed to start off a non-violent mass struggle under Gandhi’s leadership.
It is also called Wardha Proposal and Leaderless Revolt.
Gandhi gave the ultimatum ‘Do or Die’ and told the British to quit and leave India in God’s hand.
Repressive policy of the govt. and indiscriminate arrest of the leaders provoked people to violence.
Nehru was kept in Almora Jail, Gandhi in Agha Khan’s palace, Poona and Maulana Azad in Bankura.
Govt. lost control in many areas and people established Swaraj. Parallel govt’s were established.
Underground revolutionary activities started by certain leaders such as Jaiprakash Narain and Ramanandand Mishra escaped from Hazaribagh Jail and organized underground movement.
In Bombay, Aruna Asaf Ali and Congress Radio was established with Usha Mehta as its announcer and Rammanohar Lohia in Bihar.
School and college students and women actively participated, workers went on strike. There were no communal clashes during the movement.
The merchant community and capitalist did not participate.
Muslim League did not participate and the Hindu Mahasabha condemned the movement.
Communist Party did not support the movement.
Also, Rajagopalachari did not participate.
Gandhi undertook a 21 day fast between 10th Feb- 7th March 1943 for condemning the violence to the people during the Quit India movement.
Demand for Pakistan
Mohammed Iqbal in 1930 suggested for the first time the frontier province- Sindh, Baluchistan and Kashmir be made a Muslim state within the Indian federation.
Chaudhary Rehmat Ali coined the term ‘Pakistan’.
Jinnah feared the subjugation of Muslims by Hindu’s in free India and he demanded for the creation of Pakistan.
Muslim League first pass the proposal of separate Pakistan in its Lahore session in 1940 called Jinnah’s Two Nation Theory.
It was drafted by Sikandar Hayat Khan, moved by Fazlul Haq and seconded by Khaliquzzaman.
It rejected the federal scheme envisaged in the govt. of India act 1935.
In the Karachi session, Dec. 1943, the Muslim League adopted the slogan – Divide and Quit.
Rajagopalachari Formula (1944)
He proposed that a commission could be appointed for the demarcating district in the northwest and east, where Muslims were in absolute majority.
Plebiscite would be held on the basis of adult suffrage, that would decide the issue of separation from Hindustan.
If majority decide in favor of forming a separate sovereign state then such could be accepted.
Jinnah objected it as he wanted Congress to accept Two Nation theory.
He wanted only Muslims of the northwest and east to vote in the plebiscite.
Desai – Liaqat Pact (1945)
Desai being the leader of the Congress in the Central Assembly gave proposal to Liaqat Ali for the formation of Interim Government at centre.
Desai- Liaqat Proposals was attempt to appease the league leaders and find a way out of the 1942-45 political deadlock.

It was a draft proposal for formation of an interim government whereby Congress and League nominees were to have equal representation in the Central Legislature and 20% of seats were reserved for minorities.
No settlement reached.
Wavell Plan 1945
It was proposed by Lord Wavell.
It suggested to set up a new executive council with only Indian members.
The viceroy and commander in chief would be the only non-Indian members of the council.
It would work under the existing constitution but there was scope for discussion of new constitution.
Hindu’s and Muslim’s would have equal representation.
Jinnah demanded ML to have absolute choice to choose Muslim members so he rejected the plan.
Indian National Army
First conceived by Mohan Singh in Malaya, an Indian officer of the British Indian Army.
The Japanese handed over the Indian prisoners of war to Mohan Singh and he recruited them into the INA.
By 1942, 40,000 men were in the INA.
In March 1942, conference of India was held in Tokyo and Indian Independence League was formed.
The Bangkok conference, Rash Behari Bose was elected president of the league.
Subhash Bose escape to Berlin in 1941 and set up Indian League there.
He arrived at Singapore in 1943.
He left the Congress after having differences with Gandhi.
He formed the Forward Bloc in 1939.
In Singapore, he was assisted by Rash Behari Bose.
He set up a provisional Indian govt.in Oct 1943 with headquarters at Rangoon and Singapore.
The INA commanders PK Sehgal , Shah Nawaz and Gurbaksh Dhillon were put on trial at the Red Fort.
Defence of INA prisioners in the court was organized by Bhulabhai Desai, Tej Bahadur Sapru, Kailash Nath Katju, Nehru and Asaf Ali.
Muslim League also joined the country wide protests and 12th Nov.1945 was celebrated as INA day.
Cabinet Mission 1946

The Attlee govt. announced in Feb.1946 the decision to send a high powered mission of ‘Three’ British cabinet members- Pethick Lawrence, Secretary of state for India; Stafford Cripps, President of the board of trade and AV Alexander, first Lord of Admiralty to India.
They were to find out ways and means to negotiate peaceful transfer of power to India.
The British wanted united India and rejected the demand for separate Pakistan.
The Congress demanded that power be transferred to one centre and that minorities demands be worked out only after the British left India.
Congress and Muslim League differed on the issue.
Interim Government 1946
Interim govt. headed by JL Nehru was sworn in on 2nd Sept.1946.
ML refused to join initially.
Wavell persuaded the League to join in Oct.1946.
Liaqat Ali Khan of ML was made the Finance minister.
The constituent assembly began its session on 9th Dec.1946 and Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected its President, the League did not attend.
Attlee’s Statement
On 20th Feb.1947 British PM Clement Attlee announced that power would be transferred to India before 30th June 1948, even if the Indian politicians had not agreed by that time on the constitution.
Mountbatten was to replace Wavell as the viceroy.
Partition of the country was implicit in the provision that if the constituent assembly was not fully representative, than power would be transferred to more than one central govts.
Mountbatten Plan
On 3rd June 1947, Viceroy Mountbatten announced that two dominions and two constituent assemblies would be created, it is known as Third June Plan.
The plan declared that power would be handed over by 15th August 1947.
The referendum in NWFP decided in favor of Pakistan.
Princely states were given the option to join either of the two dominions or remain independent.
Boundary commission was to be set up if partition was effected.
Mountbatten’s formula was to divide India but retain unity.
The legislative assemblies of Punjab and Bengal decided in favor of partition and thus, east Bengal and West Punjab joined Pakistan.
Referendum in Sylhet resulted in the incorporation of that district in East Bengal.
Indian Independence Act 1947
The British Parliament ratified the Mountbatten plan on 18th July 1947 as the Independence of India Act, 1947.
The act provided for the creation of two independent dominions of India and Pakistan.
Each dominion was to have a governor general for effective operation of the act.
Sovereignty of British power was to be abolished.
Independence of India
On 15th August 1947, India got independence.
Lord Mountbatten continued as the Governor general of India.
Jinnah was the first Governor general of Pakistan.
Assembly and councils of the states were to be automatically dissolved.
For the transitional period, till a new constitution was adopted by each dominion, the govt. of the two dominion were to be carried on in accordance with the govt.of India act 1935.
Freedom Struggle-Various Stages
PARTITION OF BENGAL
INTRODUCTION
The 1905 Partition of Bengal, announced by Lord Curzon on July 20 and effective from October 16, separated eastern Muslim-majority areas from western Hindu-majority areas.
Meant for administrative efficiency, but actually to divide and weaken the surging nationalist movement.
This started the mass Swadeshi movement, leading to widespread protests, boycotts of British goods, and eventually the partition's annulment in 1911.
Key Aspects for Mains:
Official Reasons: Bengal was too large (78+ million people) to govern effectively (administrative efficiency) and required development of eastern regions.
Real Motives (Divide & Rule): The partition aimed to destroy the base of Bengali nationalism by creating a wedge between Hindus and Muslims.
It aimed to make Bengalis a minority in their own province by merging them with Bihar/Orissa, and it split Bengal into Hindu-majority West and Muslim-majority East (Dacca as capital).
Impact on Nationalist Movement:
Swadeshi and Boycott Movement: Widespread national protest to boycott British goods and promote indigenous industries.
Rise of Extremism: The methods of the moderate-led Indian National Congress proved ineffective, causing a shift toward extreme methods led by Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Lajpat Rai.
Communal Split: The British encouraged a Muslim separatist stance, leading to the formation of the Muslim League in 1906.
Cultural Awakening: Protests included singing Vande Mataram, wearing local textiles, and the "Raksha Bandhan" ceremony to symbolise unity, often spearheaded by leaders like Rabindranath Tagore.
Annulment (1911): Due to intense political opposition and unrest, Lord Hardinge revoked the partition.
However, to appease communal divides, Bengal was re-divided into linguistic provinces (Bihar and Orissa separated), and the capital was shifted from Calcutta to Delhi.

Conclusion: While the partition was intended to break the nationalist spirit, it actually served as a turning point that accelerated Indian national consciousness and propelled the freedom struggle into a more intense phase.
SWADESHI AND BOYCOTT MOVEMENT
INTRODUCTION
The Swadeshi and Boycott movement (1905–1908) was a pivotal, organized campaign against the 1905 Partition of Bengal by Lord Curzon.
It promoted indigenous industries and goods (Swadeshi) while boycotting British goods, schools, and courts to cripple British economic interests and foster self-reliance (Atma-shakti).
Led by leaders like Tilak and Tagore, it ignited mass nationalism, though it waned by 1908 due to repression and internal divisions.
Key Aspects of the Movement:
Origin: Launched formally on August 7, 1905, at Calcutta Town Hall to protest the partition of Bengal.
Methods: Boycott of British goods (cloth, salt), public burning of foreign items, use of Swadeshi goods, promoting national education, and fostering self-reliance.
Forms of Protest: Singing Vande Mataram, tying Rakhis as a symbol of unity, and organizing hartals (strikes).

Spread: While centered in Bengal, the movement spread to other parts of India, including Bombay and Pune (led by Bal Gangadhar Tilak), Punjab (Lala Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh), and Madras (Chidambaram Pillai).
Key leaders included Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, Lala Lajpat Rai, and Aurobindo Ghosh.
Impact:
Economic: Encouraged the growth of indigenous industries such as textile mills, soap factories, and match factories.
Cultural: Led to a boom in national literature, songs (like Rabindranath Tagore's Amar Sonar Bangla), and art.
Political: Transformed the national movement from moderate petitions to passive resistance, laying the groundwork for larger movements.

The movement saw intense British repression, including the banning of meetings and media censorship, causing it to lose momentum by 1908, but it significantly increased the momentum of the fight for Swaraj.
Approach of Nationalists during Swadeshi Movement

Moderates leaders: The moderates began to criticise the partition scheme ever since it was announced; they initially thought that the British would accept their arguments, which they presented through petitions, prayers and public meetings.
Education:
Carlyle Circular: In October 1905, Carlyle, the Chief Secretary of the Government of Bengal, issued an infamous circular that posed a threat to student picketers.
The circular warned of withdrawing grants, scholarships, and institutional affiliations from students involved in protests against the British government.
The boycott of schools and colleges compelled leaders to consider establishing a parallel education system in Bengal.

These led to the founding of the Bengal Technical Institute, the Bengal National College and School (1906 with Aurobindo Ghosh, Principal), and several national primary and secondary schools in the districts.
Industries: A number of exclusive Indian industrial ventures such as Bengal Chemicals, Bangel Lakshmi Cotton Mills, Mohini Mills and National Tannery, were started.
Key Leaders in the Swadeshi Movement:
Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, Lala Lajpat Rai, Aurobindo Ghosh, Surendranath Banerjee, Rabindranath Tagore, VO Chidambaram Pillai.
The moderate nationalist opinion:
Surendranath Banerjee, Krishnakumar Mitra, and Narendra Kumar Sen were prominent figures.
Despite their strong belief in British justice, they were cautious not to escalate the agitation too far.

Social reformist aimed at gathering national strength through a persistent movement of self-help and self-reliance by organising indigenous enterprises, nationalistic educational processes and setting up village uplift societies to bridge the gulf between the rural and urban people.
Rise of Extremists during Swadeshi Movement

Extremists found expression in periodicals like New India (edited by Bepinchandra Pal), Bande Mataram (edited by Aurobindo Ghosh), Sandhya (edited by Brahmabandhav Upadhyaya) and Yugantar (edited by Bhupendranath Dutta).
They demanded self-government for India, not under British Paramountcy (as the moderates wished), but by severing all British connections and wiping off all British influences.
The extremist leaders passionately advocated for Swaraj and explored various strategies to attain it.
They sought to expand boycott techniques beyond British goods and educational institutions to other domains.
Participation of People in Swadeshi Movement
The Congress, including both Moderates and Radicals, united in opposition to it.
They orchestrated large public gatherings, and demonstrations and devised innovative methods of mass protest.
The unfolding struggle was named the Swadeshi movement, with its strongest impact felt in Bengal but also resonating in other regions; in Andhra, it was referred to as the Vandemataram Movement.
All-India Aspect of the Swadeshi Movement
The call for Swadeshi and Swaraj resonated in other provinces of India too.
Movements supporting Bengal's unity and boycotting foreign goods were organised in Bombay, Madras, and northern India.
Tilak played a prominent role in spreading the Swadeshi movement across the country.
Swadeshi Movement Consequences
The Swadeshi movement had significant long-term economic and social consequences such as:
It led to the revival of domestic cottage industries and handicrafts, which were declining under British industrial policies favouring imported machine-made goods.
The production of indigenous textiles, soaps, matches and other daily-use items received a boost.
Swadeshi enterprises promoted Indian entrepreneurship and technical skills.
Socially, it inculcated a spirit of pride in local products and craftsmanship.
The involvement of students, women, peasants, and artisans, along with the middle class, fostered wider participation that bridged urban-rural divides.

While the Swadeshi agitation did not radically overturn British economic dominance, it laid the groundwork for the growth of an indigenous industrial and economic base aligned with national interests.
The Swadeshi movement was also responsible for the spread of national ideas beyond the official and elite circles.
Nationalism became a political movement.
Several million Indians settled abroad also became involved in the movement.
A new generation of Indian politicians emerged.
The aftermath movement led to the unification of desperate political identities shaped by public activism, which influenced most of the national leaders.
Reversal of Bengal Partition: In response to growing opposition and administrative difficulties, the partition was annulled by Lord Hardinge in 1911.
Swadeshi Movement Evaluation
It led to the beginning of the organised political movement in India.
It marked a total reversal of the earlier nationalist approach of "petitioning and praying", as well as a virtual rejection of the moderate political programme.
It set before the Indian people the goal of Swaraj or independence and committed them to the task of doing away with Britain's imperialist stranglehold over India.
In the pursuit of Swaraj, it advocated "passive resistance" or civil disobedience against British authority.
The Swadeshi movement, although not a full-fledged mass uprising, exhibited some secretive aspects and revealed certain weaknesses.
However, it achieved significant success in terms of ideology, organisation, and political strategies.
NON-COOPERATION MOVEMENT
Introduction
The Non-Cooperation Movement was the first nationwide movement launched by Gandhi in 1920 to mobilise the Indian masses to peacefully resist British rule in India.
It emerged as a powerful and fervent response to a culmination of grievances and disillusionment that had been building up among the Indian populace.
Rowlatt Act and the brutal Jallianwala Bagh Massacre were the immediate causes for launching the movement.
Congress, at its special session of Calcutta in September 1920, approved the Non-Cooperation movement, which was later endorsed by the Nagpur session of Congress in December 1920.
The movement saw tremendous participation of masses throughout the country.
However, the movement was called off by Gandhi on February 11, 1922, following the Chauri Chaura incident in the Gorakhpur district of Uttar Pradesh.
Non-Cooperation Movement
During the years 1920-21, the Indian National Movement entered a new phase of mass politics and mobilisation.
Two mass movements, Khilafat and Non-Cooperation, were formed to oppose British rule.
The Non-Cooperation Movement was launched in 1920 to mobilise the Indian masses to peacefully resist British rule through non-cooperation with British institutions, laws, and policies.
Both the Khilafat Movement and Mahatma Gandhi's Non-Cooperation Movement saw a convergence at the end of the summer of 1920.
Gandhi, through his earlier localised movements such as Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad, had already gained popularity and was able to attract the masses throughout the country.
Thus transitioning to a new era of nationwide movement and mass politics.
Causes of Non-Cooperation Movement
Simmering dissent: The economic exploitation of India by the British colonial rulers had already impoverished the masses.
The economic and political situation of the country during and after the First World War was further aggravated by rising high inflation, heavy taxation and forced cultivation of cash crops.
First World War: The British government backtracked on its promises to consider nationalist demands in exchange for Indian support in the War.

Montague-Chelmsford reforms: The reforms introduced by the British government through the Montague-Chelmsford in the form of the Government of India Act 1919 fell short of Indian aspirations for self-governance and responsible government.
The vast majority of leaders called it "disappointing and unsatisfactory."
Rowlatt Act: It was passed in 1919 that allowed for the arrest and detention of Indians without trial.
Its primary goal was to imprison nationalists without allowing them to defend themselves.
This had infuriated the nationalists and other leaders.
Gandhi decided to use Satyagraha to oppose it.

Jallianwala Bagh Massacre: The Jallianwala Bagh Massacre in Amritsar, in which British troops opened fire on a peaceful gathering of Indians, killing hundreds, shocked and enraged the Indian population.
Khilafat Movement: The Khilafat Movement was a parallel movement initiated by Indian Muslims to protest against the dismantling of the Ottoman Caliphate by the British after the First World War.
Gandhi supported the Khilafat cause and advocated for non-cooperation.
Non-Cooperation Movement Timeline
As a follow-up to the Rowlatt Act, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, and the Khilafat Movement, Mahatma Gandhi announced his intention to begin Non-Cooperation with the Government.
At a special session in Calcutta in September 1920, Congress approved a Non-Cooperation Movement until the Punjab and Khilafat wrongs were corrected and Swaraj was established.
The programme of non-cooperation was accepted and endorsed without opposition in the Nagpur INC Session of December 1920.
Non-Cooperation Movement Features
The Non-Cooperation Movement, launched by Mahatma Gandhi in 1920, was a significant phase in the Indian independence struggle.
The following are some key features:
Non-violent Protest: The movement emphasised non-violence and civil disobedience.
Surrender of Titles and Honorary Positions: Individuals were encouraged to surrender their titles and honorary positions conferred by the British government.

Swaraj: The Indian National Congress, under the leadership of Gandhi, adopted the objective of attaining Swaraj (self-government) through peaceful and legitimate means as part of the Non-Cooperation Movement.

Gandhi planned the movement in stages: initially non-cooperation (boycotts, resignations, etc.), and if Swaraj was not achieved or if the government responded with repression, the movement would escalate to civil disobedience and non-payment of taxes.
Resignation from Government Positions and Local Bodies: People were urged to resign from government jobs and memberships of local bodies.
Boycott of Foreign Goods: Indians were encouraged to boycott British goods and use only Indian-made products.
Foreign-made clothing was gathered and set ablaze.

Boycott of Elections: Indians were asked to boycott elections held in accordance with the provisions of the 1919 Act, as well as legislative councils (though there were differences over this boycott).
Boycott of law-courts was also encouraged.
Non-cooperation with Government Institutions: This included boycotting courts, government functions, and legal practices, as well as government schools and colleges.
Refusal to Serve in the British Army: People were encouraged not to serve in the British army.
Non-payment of Taxes: If the above steps did not yield results, people were prepared to refuse to pay taxes.
Promotion of Swadeshi Principles: The movement promoted the adoption of Swadeshi principles, including hand spinning and weaving (Charkha and Khadi).
Thousands of volunteers went door-to-door persuading people to adopt Swadeshi goods.
Boycott Movement Against Liquor and Toddy Shops: The boycott extended to liquor and toddy shops.
Establishment of National Institutions: National schools, colleges, and private panchayat courts were established.
Institutions like Kashi Vidyapeeth, Bihar Vidyapeeth, and Jamia Millia Islamia were founded.
Establishment of Panchayats for settling disputes: The movement promoted the establishment of local Panchayats to resolve disputes.
Unity of Congress and Muslim League: The movement saw a rare unity between the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League.
Maintenance of Hindu-Muslim Unity and Strict Non-violence: There was a focus on maintaining Hindu-Muslim unity and practicing strict non-violence.
Jail Bharo Andolan: Congress volunteers promoted the Charkha and Khadi and participated in the "Jail Bharo Andolan" (fill the jails movement).
Tilak Swaraj Fund: Gandhi announced the Tilak Swaraj Fund, which aimed at collecting Rs 1 crore to aid constructive work.
The movement was called off in 1922 following the Chauri Chaura incident, but it played a crucial role in mobilizing the Indian masses against British rule.
Non-Cooperation Movement Withdrawal
The non-cooperation movement was one of the most powerful movements in the Indian freedom struggle.
However, despite all efforts, it was called off by Gandhiji due to various reasons.
These reasons include:
Chauri-Chaura Incident: In Chauri-Chaura, Uttar Pradesh, a group of protestors attacked and set fire to a police station, resulting in the death of several police officers.
Gandhi felt that the incident violated the principle of non-violence, and as a result, he called off the movement in February 1922.
Lack of discipline and violence: Mahatma Gandhi realised that the Indian masses were not fully prepared for a nationwide struggle of civil disobedience and non-cooperation.
There were instances of indiscipline and violence by some participants.
For instance, the Mopillah revolt in Kerala turned violent.
Abolishment of Caliphate: Khilafat, one of the non-cooperation movement's issues, lost its relevance.
Turks themselves, under the leadership of Mustafa Kemal, first abolished the Ottoman sultanate in 1922 and then did away with the office of the Khalifa in 1924.
Rise of militancy: Towards the later stages of the movements, there was a gradual shift towards more radical and militant approaches.
This led to a loss of popular support and alienation of certain sections of society.
Government repression: The British colonial government had responded to the Non-Cooperation Movement with harsh measures.
The government seemed in no mood for negotiations.
Volunteer corps were declared illegal, public meetings were forbidden, the press was silenced, and most leaders of the Congress were arrested.
Non-Cooperation Movement Significance
Though the non-cooperation movement did not succeed and was suddenly called off, it had a significant impact on the Indian freedom struggle.
It played a significant role in generating and spreading anti-imperialist consciousness among Indian people.
Hindu-Muslim unity: Gandhi opined that the realisation of Swarajya lies in the proper resolution of the Mohammedan question.
This effort led to Hindu-Muslim unity, reflected in the ensuing mass mobilisations against colonial rule.
Issue of social justice: The non-cooperation movement introduced the issue of caste discrimination and untouchability to national politics and made Gandhi an important leader for social justice.
Mass participation: The Khilafat and NCM witnessed extensive participation from the Indian masses from all walks of life, including peasants, workers, students, teachers, women and professionals.
The long-standing grievances of the working masses against the British, as well as the Indian masters, were given an outlet through this movement.
Gandhi’s emphasis on non-violence introduced women in large numbers into the freedom struggle.
Thus, it proved to be a mass mobilisation in the true sense.
National consciousness: The most significant success of the movement was the creation of political and social consciousness and nationalism in Indians.
Inspiration for subsequent movements: The success and impact of these movements paved the way for subsequent movements such as the Civil Disobedience Movement and the Quit India Movement.
Non-Cooperation Movement Limitations
The Non-Cooperation Movement was a significant step in India's struggle for independence.
However, it had several limitations and challenges that impacted its effectiveness.

Merger of Khilafat issue: The cause of the Khilafat movement was exclusively on the religious line, and then the convergence of NCM and Khilafat proved to be less useful for secular politics in India in the long term.
Limited reach: While the Non-Cooperation Movement garnered substantial support, especially in urban areas, it did not have universal backing across India.
The rural population had limited awareness of these movements and often remained detached.
Lack of clear goal: The movements didn't have a well-defined roadmap beyond non-cooperation with the British for achieving independence or addressing broader socio-economic issues.
Differences: There were differences in strategies, ideologies, and priorities that led to fragmentation and weakened the overall effectiveness of the movements.
For example, there were differences regarding the boycott of legislative councils.
Some leaders, such as C.R. Das, were unwilling to include a council boycott.
CIVIL DISOBEDIENCE MOVEMENT
Civil Disobedience Movement was started by Mahatma Gandhi on 12th March 1930 against the salt tax imposed by the British.

Civil Disobedience Movement(1930) is regarded as the second major mass movement and a distinct advancement in widening the social reach of India's struggle for freedom after the Non-Cooperation Movement.
Known also as Salt Satyagraha, it was also the first time when Congress put the objective of complete independence to the British authority as well as to the Indian masses.
The Civil Disobedience Movement was formally launched by Mahatma Gandhi on 6th April 1930 by breaking salt law after his historic Dandi March.
It was followed by the widespread arrest of national leaders throughout the nation.
Background of Civil Disobedience Movement
The primary factors that contributed to the conditions for the Civil Disobedience Movement included:
protests against the arrest of revolutionary leaders,
India's pursuit of its constitution,
and a growing demand for complete independence following the rejection of Dominion status as proposed in the Nehru Report.
A clash between factions led to a one-year grace period for the British to grant Dominion status by December 31, 1929, or face a Civil Disobedience Movement.
Irwin’s Declaration (October 1929): Viceroy Lord Irwin promised Dominion status and a Round Table Conference post-Simon Commission's report.
The lack of a timeline frustrated Congress, leading to the Purna Swaraj resolution.
Lahore Session (1929) and Purna Swaraj:
Jawaharlal Nehru led the session, emphasizing Purna Swaraj.

Key decisions included declaring complete independence, hoisting the tricolour on December 31, 1929, boycotting Round Table Conferences, taking the Independence Day pledge on January 26, 1930, and launching the Civil Disobedience Movement under Gandhi.
Gandhi’s Eleven Demands
Gandhi's demands were a compromise formula that appealed to a wide range of political opinions.
He gave the British until January 31, 1930, to accept or reject the demands.
If the demands were not met by March 11, Gandhi threatened civil disobedience.
DEMANDS
Reduce rupee-sterling ratio.
Agricultural tax by 50% and make it a subject of legislative control
Eliminate the government's monopoly on salt and abolish the salt tax
Reduce military expenditure and salaries of highest-grade services
Release all political prisoners
Reform in the Criminal Investigation Department
Accept Postal Reservation Bill
Protect Indian Textiles
Prohibition of intoxicants
Reserve coastal shipping for Indians
Allow popular control of the issue of firearm licences.
Launch of Civil Disobedience Movement
With no response from the government regarding the 11 demands, Gandhi decided to launch the Civil Disobedience Movement.
Among all the demands, he chose to violate the salt law because the British were inhumanely taxing this basic necessary item and had a near monopoly over it.
It was a brilliant plan, though only a few could grasp its significance at the time of its announcement.
Dandi March
Gandhi announced the ‘Dandi March’ after informing Irwin in advance that he would break the salt laws.
Gandhi and his 78 supporters started the march from Ahmedabad to the Dandi coast on March 12, 1930, and reached it on April 5, 1930.
He broke the salt regulations on April 6 and, thus, officially started the Civil Disobedience Movement.
After breaking the Salt Law, Mahatma Gandhi declared, “Sedition has become my religion”
Form of protest:
Breaking of salt laws.
Picketing of liquor and foreign cloth shops.
Refusing to pay taxes.
Giving up law practice.
Boycotting courts by refraining from litigation.
Resignation by government servants from their posts.
Adherence to the truth and non-violence as means to attain Swaraj.
Obedience of the local leaders after Gandhi’s arrest.
Truce period

Tribal and Peasant militancy, Congress leaders being in jail, and decreasing support of rich peasants as well as business classes in the later months of 1930 compelled Gandhi and Congress to retreat from the Movement.
Gandhi-Irwin Pact
The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was an agreement signed on March 5, 1931, between Gandhi and Lord Irwin, the then Viceroy of India.
It marked the end of the Civil Disobedience Movement's first phase.
The key provisions included the release of political prisoners, the right to make salt for personal use, and the withdrawal of ordinances against civil disobedience.
In return, Gandhi agreed to suspend the movement and attend the Second Round Table Conference in London.
Karachi Session, 1931
The Karachi Session of the Congress held in March 1931 aimed to endorse the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
Withdrawal of Civil Disobedience Movement
The Civil Disobedience Movement was initially withdrawn in 1931 after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
However, following the Second Round Table Conference's failure, Gandhi resumed the movement.
Arrested in January 1932, he faced severe repression, including confiscation of Congress funds and occupation of buildings.
Despite initial momentum, the movement began to decline due to intense government repression.
By late 1932, it was tapering off but continued in some form until 1934.
Gandhi, still in jail, suspended the movement in May 1933 and formally withdrew it in April 1934.
Civil Disobedience Movement Participation
The Civil Disobedience Movement saw diverse participation from various social groups, each contributing uniquely to the struggle against British rule.
Women, peasants, students, and merchants played key roles in shaping its course.
Urban areas: In the urban areas, the support for Gandhian ideology was less than that during the NCM.
Only a few lawyers gave up their practice, and a few students joined ‘national schools’ instead of government-controlled institutions.
This was due to perhaps the popularity of revolutionary nationalists (especially Bhagat Singh).
Muslims: Muslim participation was nowhere near the NCM, and there was even communal discontent in some places.
Merchants: There was solidarity with the nationalist movement.
Business class and Merchants: Business groups showed considerable support during the initial phase that filled the gap of other sections, especially Gujarati business communities.
Women: Women were active in picketing outside liquor stores, opium dens, and shops selling foreign clothing.
It was a liberating experience for them.
Peasants: Peasants organised numerous protests against the policies of the British Government and took part in them in large numbers.
Tribal: During the Civil Disobedience movement, tribal people launched a non-violent protest (or Satyagraha) against these imposed restrictions.
Students: The Civil Disobedience Movement was heavily influenced by students and youth.
They organised protests, strikes, and boycotts, and they took an active role in the Salt Satyagraha.
Civil Disobedience Movement Assessment
Despite not achieving its goals of, Purna Swaraj, the Movement occupies a special place in the history of India’s quest for freedom.
Not a failure for Congress: Congress could mobilise great political support and got moral authority that was reflected in the massive victory in the 1937 election.
QUIT INDIA MOVEMENT
INTRODUCTION

The Quit India Movement (August 1942), or August Kranti, was a pivotal mass uprising initiated by Gandhi following the failure of the Cripps Mission, demanding an immediate end to British rule under the slogan "Do or Die."
Marked by widespread, leaderless protests and parallel governments, it signified the final, intensive push for independence.
Background of Quit India Movement 1942

The background of the Quit India Movement lies in the failure of the Cripps Mission, economic hardships during World War II, and rising nationalist sentiments from earlier movements like Civil Disobedience and the demand for Purna Swaraj.
With Britain weakened by the war, Gandhi launched the movement in 1942, urging Indians to "Do or Die" for independence.
It has four main features:
Accommodative of violence against the state,
Aimed at destroying the British rule involving anybody believing in complete independence instead of trained satyagrahis,
Students were called to play the major role and should lead the Movement after the arrest of senior Congress leaders and total defiance of government authority.
Key Aspects:
Causes: Failure of the Cripps Mission (1942), rising economic distress (inflation/scarcity), Japanese expansion in Southeast Asia, and the need to end colonial rule.
Unique Features:
Once the main leaders were arrested on 9 August, the Movement took a radical turn, often cited as the most ‘un-Gandhian’ method of the freedom movement.
Underground Activity: Led by leaders like Jayaprakash Narayan, Aruna Asaf Ali, and Usha Mehta.
Parallel Governments: Established in areas like Tamluk (Bengal), Satara (Maharashtra), and Ballia (UP).
Mass Participation: Active involvement of youth, women, and workers.
Spread of the Quit India Movement 1942
Quit India Movement had two phases: the mass movement phase (August to September 1942), and the quasi-guerrilla insurgency phase (afterwards).
The people started burning and destroying anything that symbolised British authority, such as post offices, police stations, government buildings, railways and telegraph lines.
The scale of participation in Bihar and eastern UP was unparalleled.
Limitations of the Quit India Movement 1942
While the Quit India Movement played a crucial role in India's struggle for independence, it also had several limitations that affected its overall impact.
Failed to meet its objectives: The movement did not immediately lead to freedom, and it took more years of struggle and negotiations before independence was achieved.
Lack of central leadership: This hindered effective coordination and decision-making, leading to confusion and fragmentation within the movement.
No consensus:  Some political parties and leaders opposed the Quit India Movement.
Muslim League and bureaucracy was also against the Movement.
B. R. Ambedkar and Periyar were also against the Movement.
Communal divide: Muslim participation in the movement was even lower than the CDM.
Jinnah appealed to Muslims to join the armed forces.
Muslim League used this time period to mobilise masses that helped it in the next elections of 1945-46, which strengthened its demand of a separate state, ultimately resulting in the Partition.
Further, there were some areas of communal violence during the Movement.
Significance of the Quit India Movement 1942
The Quit India Movement, active until 1944, was ultimately suppressed by the British.
Although it did not immediately achieve its goal of driving out the British, it was a defining phase in India’s struggle for independence.

A Radical and Widespread Movement: The Quit India Movement was marked by unprecedented enthusiasm, surpassing earlier movements like the Non-Cooperation Movement (NCM) and the Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM).
Unlike the urban-focused NCM and broader CDM, it was the most radical and violent, driven largely by the poor and labour classes, who were severely affected by wartime inflation.

Mass Participation and Grassroots Leadership: Despite the absence of central leadership, it witnessed massive participation from diverse groups, including younger generations, peasants, tribals, and women.
The movement had a grassroots character, with a bottom-up approach led by the subaltern classes, making it a true people's movement.
Role of Emerging Leaders: Leaders of the Congress Socialist Party, such as Jayaprakash Narayan and Ram Manohar Lohia, played a crucial role in mobilizing the masses.
The movement also saw the rise of new leaders like Aruna Asaf Ali, who became an enduring symbol of resistance.
Impact on the British Rule: While it did not force an immediate British exit, the movement weakened their authority and control.
It set the tone for subsequent protests, including the public response during the INA Trials, and created momentum contributing to India’s eventual independence.
British Response to Quit India Movement 1942

The British responded to the Quit India Movement with swift repression, by arresting key Congress leaders like Gandhi, Nehru, and Patel, detaining over 100,000 people, and declaring the Congress unlawful.
Violent clashes led to significant casualties, with deaths ranging from 1,028 to over 10,000.

The British, supported by the Viceroy's Council, the All India Muslim League, Hindu Mahasabha, princely states, Indian Imperial Police, and British Indian Army, used raids and force to suppress the movement.
Despite this, the economic disruption and political pressure reinforced the inevitability of India's independence.
Conclusion:

Though the British suppressed the uprising by 1944, the movement shifted the political landscape from negotiating for reforms to an unstoppable momentum toward complete independence, ultimately leading to India’s sovereignty.
ROLE OF WOMEN IN FREEDOM STRUGGLE
INTRODUCTION
Women played a pivotal, transformative role in the Indian freedom struggle, transitioning from domestic spheres to active mass participation, particularly under Gandhian leadership.

Their contributions included organizing boycotts (Swadeshi), leading Satyagraha’s (Salt Satyagraha), engaging in revolutionary activities, and managing underground movements, significantly broadening the social base of the nationalist movement.
Key Phases and Contributions
Early Phase & 1857 Revolt: Women such as Rani Lakshmi Bai, Begum Hazrat Mahal showcased early armed resistance against British colonial rule.
Swadeshi Movement (1905-1911): Women participated by boycotting foreign goods, picketing shops, and promoting the use of indigenous products (Khadi).
Gandhian Phase (1920-1947): Gandhi enabled mass mobilization, seeing women’s "moral courage" as ideal for Satyagraha.
They were crucial in:
Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22): Active picketing and promotion of khadi.
Civil Disobedience/Salt Satyagraha (1930): Sarojini Naidu led the Dharsana Satyagraha; women marched and manufactured salt.
Quit India Movement (1942): Women like Usha Mehta ran secret underground radio stations (Congress Radio).
Revolutionary Activities: Women participated in armed struggle, such as Pritilata Wodeyar leading the Chittagong European Club raid, and Suniti Choudhury/Santi Ghose assassinating a magistrate.
Impact on Society
Beyond Household: Women stepped into public life, breaking traditional social barriers.
Gender Equality: The struggle paved the way for women's empowerment and leadership in independent India.
Unity: The, symbolizing "Bharat Mata," acted as a unifying force, strengthening national sentiment.
STUDENT’S ROLE IN FREEDOM STRUGGLE
Students played a pivotal role in the Indian freedom struggle by accelerating mass movements, promoting indigenous goods, and engaging in revolutionary activities.

They formed the backbone of agitations during the Swadeshi, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, and Quit India movements, acting as messengers, protesters, and agents of social change to challenge British colonial rule.
Key Aspects of Student Participation

Early Movements & Activism: Students were inspired by leaders like Tilak and Aurobindo Ghosh, especially during the 1905 Partition of Bengal, where they boycotted British educational institutions and promoted swadeshi goods.

Establishment of Independent Institutions: To counter British education, students and leaders established national institutions like Jamia Millia Islamia, Kashi Vidyapeeth, and Bengal National College.
Key Movements Participation:
Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22): Thousands of students left government schools and colleges, participating in strikes and organizing picketing.
Civil Disobedience Movement (1930): Students played a significant role in organizing, acting as picketers for liquor and foreign cloth shops, and assisting in salt satyagraha.
Quit India Movement (1942): Students were in the forefront of the violence-prone phase of this movement, holding strikes and protests after senior leaders were arrested.

Revolutionary Activities: Students were active participants in secret revolutionary societies like the Anushilan Samiti and Yugantar in Bengal, as well as the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) in Northern India.
Ideological Shift: The student movement grew in strength, with formal organizations like the All India Students Federation (AISF) formed in 1936 to organize student campaigns against the British.
Social Reform: Beyond politics, students were active in addressing social evils like untouchability, casteism, and illiteracy.

THIRD BATTLE OF PANIPAT 1761

The Third Battle of Panipat was fought on January 14, 1761, between the Maratha Empire and the Afghan forces led by Ahmad Shah Durrani (Abdali), resulting in a decisive Afghan victory and a significant check to Maratha expansion in North India.
This battle was fought in Panipat (Haryana) because of its geographical significance as a gateway to the Indo-Gangetic plains, offering a perfect, open terrain for massive, decisive battles.
Key Aspects for Mains:
Participants: Marathas (led by Sadashivrao Bhau) vs. Afghan Durrani Empire (led by Ahmad Shah Abdali).

The Afghans were supported by Indian allies, specifically Najib-ud-Daula (Rohilla) and Shuja-ud-Daula (Nawab of Oudh), while the Marathas were unable to secure support from key local powers like the Sikhs, Jats, or Rajputs.
Significance of the Site: Panipat, situated near the Yamuna River and north of Delhi, controlled the Grand Trunk Road and offered a strategic position for conducting large-scale military maneuvers.

Causes of the War: The rapid expansion of the Maratha Empire into Northern India, reaching the Punjab-Afghanistan border, brought them into direct conflict with Abdali's ambition to dominate the region, which was supported by Mughals seeking to curb Maratha power.
Reasons for Maratha Defeat:
Alliances: Abdali built a strong coalition (Rohillas, Oudh), while the Marathas were largely isolated.
Supplies: Abdali cut off supplies to the Maratha camp, leading to starvation and forcing a battle.
Strategy: The Afghan army used superior logistics and artillery tactics compared to the traditional cavalry-focused Marathas.
Consequences (Post-1761):
Check on Expansion: The dream of a Maratha-led Indian empire was severely damaged, and their prestige took a major blow.
Power Vacuum: The collapse of the Marathas in the north created a vacuum that allowed the British East India Company to accelerate their expansion.
Revival: The Marathas, however, managed to make a significant recovery and regain control of Delhi within a decade under Peshwa Madhavrao.
Quick Facts:
Peshwa: Balaji Baji Rao was the Peshwa at the time, and the loss caused him immense shock.
Mughal Emperor: Shah Alam II was the reigning Mughal emperor, though the real power was contested.
Losses: It was one of the bloodiest battles of the 18th century, with an estimated 60,000–70,000 troops killed, plus a high number of civilian casualties, with many prisoners massacred.
